topics.title: System Software: Assemblers, Loaders, Linkers, Macros
topics.summary: How source text becomes a running program: assembler passes, macro expansion, linking and loading.

blocks.text:
## What system software is

Application software solves a user's problem. **System software** solves the machine's problem: it bridges the gap between the way people want to express computation and the way the hardware actually executes it. The classical members of this family are the **assembler**, the **macro processor**, the **compiler**, the **linker**, the **loader** and the operating system itself. UGC NET treats the first four as one compact block of questions, and they are cheap marks because the material is mechanical: if you know what each pass reads and what each pass writes, you can answer almost anything asked.

The pipeline for a classical compiled program is:

```
source.c --compiler--> source.asm --assembler--> obj.o --linker--> a.out --loader--> memory image
```

Each stage removes one kind of symbolic freedom. The compiler removes high-level control structures, the assembler removes mnemonics and local labels, the linker removes external symbol names, and the loader removes the last assumption — that the program starts at address 0.

## The assembler and why it needs two passes

An assembler translates one assembly statement into one machine instruction. The only genuinely hard part is the **forward reference**: a statement may use a label that is defined later.

```
      BC   GT, LOOP     ; LOOP is not known yet
...
LOOP  SUB  AREG, D
```

When the assembler reaches the branch it does not yet know the address of `LOOP`. Two designs solve this.

**Two-pass assembler.**

- *Pass 1* scans the source, maintains the **location counter (LC)**, and enters every label into the **symbol table (SYMTAB)** together with its address. It also collects literals into **LITTAB** and pool boundaries into **POOLTAB**, processes `EQU` and `DS`/`DC` to advance LC correctly, and produces an intermediate form of the source. Pass 1 generates *no* object code.
- *Pass 2* re-reads the intermediate code, looks up each symbol in the now-complete SYMTAB, consults **OPTAB** for the opcode and instruction length, and emits the object module plus relocation information.

**One-pass assembler.** It emits code immediately and, when it meets an undefined symbol, leaves a hole and chains it onto a list hanging off that symbol's SYMTAB entry. When the label is finally defined, the assembler walks the chain and fills in the address. This technique is called **backpatching**. A one-pass assembler is faster but must either load directly into memory or produce a slightly more complex object format.

blocks.title: Which table is built where
blocks.text:
| Table | Built in | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| OPTAB (mnemonic to opcode, length) | fixed, built into the assembler | pass 1 (for length) and pass 2 (for opcode) |
| SYMTAB (label to address) | pass 1 | pass 2 |
| LITTAB (literal to address) | pass 1 | pass 2 |
| POOLTAB (index of first literal of each pool) | pass 1 | pass 1 |
| Base/location counter | pass 1 | pass 1 |

The single most asked fact: **SYMTAB is built in pass 1 and consumed in pass 2**, while OPTAB is consulted in both passes but for different fields.

## Assembler directives you must be able to trace

| Directive | Meaning | Effect on LC |
|---|---|---|
| `START n` | first word is at address $n$ | LC $\leftarrow n$ |
| `END` | end of source; may name an entry point | flushes the last literal pool |
| `EQU expr` | define a symbol as the value of an expression | none |
| `ORIGIN expr` | move the location counter | LC $\leftarrow$ value of expr |
| `DS n` | declare storage: reserve $n$ words, uninitialised | LC $\leftarrow$ LC $+\;n$ |
| `DC 'v'` | declare constant: reserve and initialise | LC $\leftarrow$ LC $+\;1$ (per value) |
| `LTORG` | assemble the literals collected since the last `LTORG` here | LC advances by the pool size |

`EQU` does **not** reserve memory and does **not** advance LC — that is the classic distractor against `DC`, which does both.

blocks.title: Worked example — pass 1 location counter and symbol table
blocks.text:
Assemble this fragment (one word per instruction):

```
        START 100
        MOVER AREG, B
        ADD   AREG, ='5'
        MOVEM AREG, C
LOOP    SUB   AREG, D
        BC    GT, LOOP
        LTORG
B       DS    1
C       DS    2
D       DC    '3'
        END
```

Run the location counter:

| LC | Statement | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | `MOVER AREG, B` | B is a forward reference; LC $\to$ 101 |
| 101 | `ADD AREG, ='5'` | literal `='5'` entered in LITTAB, no address yet; LC $\to$ 102 |
| 102 | `MOVEM AREG, C` | LC $\to$ 103 |
| 103 | `SUB AREG, D` | **LOOP = 103** entered in SYMTAB; LC $\to$ 104 |
| 104 | `BC GT, LOOP` | LOOP already known; LC $\to$ 105 |
| 105 | `LTORG` | literal `='5'` gets **address 105**; LC $\to$ 106 |
| 106 | `B DS 1` | **B = 106**; LC $\to$ 107 |
| 107 | `C DS 2` | **C = 107**, occupies 107 and 108; LC $\to$ 109 |
| 109 | `D DC '3'` | **D = 109**; LC $\to$ 110 |

Final SYMTAB: LOOP 103, B 106, C 107, D 109. LITTAB: `='5'` at 105. POOLTAB holds one entry, literal index 1.

Note that `DS 2` advanced LC by two but still defined only one symbol, and that the literal was placed at the `LTORG`, not at the point of use. Both are standard question hooks.

## Macros: expansion, not call

A **macro** is a named piece of source text. When the macro processor meets an invocation it **substitutes the body inline**, with parameters textually replaced. A subroutine, by contrast, exists once in memory and is entered at run time by a call instruction.

| | Macro | Subroutine |
|---|---|---|
| When resolved | assembly time (expansion) | run time (call/return) |
| Copies in the object program | one per invocation | exactly one |
| Speed | faster: no call/return, no stack frame | slower: linkage overhead |
| Size | grows with number of uses | constant |
| Argument passing | textual substitution | registers/stack |

A macro processor keeps three tables:

- **MNT** — Macro Name Table: macro name to its index in MDT.
- **MDT** — Macro Definition Table: the stored body, with parameters replaced by positional markers such as `#1`, `#2`.
- **ALA** — Argument List Array: at expansion time, the actual arguments, so `#1` can be replaced by the real operand.

Macros also support **conditional expansion** with assembler-time statements `AIF` (conditional branch), `AGO` (unconditional branch) and `LCL`/`GBL` expansion-time variables. These are evaluated *while expanding*, so different invocations of the same macro can produce different numbers of instructions. Nested macro calls need the processor to be re-entrant or to stack its expansion state; a *nested macro definition* (a macro whose body defines another macro) is only created when the outer macro is expanded.

## Linkers and loaders

The assembler produces an object module that still contains two kinds of unfinished business: references to symbols defined in other modules (**external references**), and addresses computed on the assumption that the module begins at 0 (**relocatable addresses**).

- **Linking** resolves external references. The linker reads every module's table of definitions (ESD/EXTDEF) and references (EXTREF), assigns each module a position, and patches the references.
- **Relocation** adjusts address fields by the load-time offset. The object module carries a **relocation table** saying which fields are address-sensitive.
- **Loading** brings the final image into memory and transfers control to the entry point.

The classical loader taxonomy:

| Loader | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute loader | loads at the address the assembler assumed; no relocation, no linking | simplest; program cannot move |
| Bootstrap loader | tiny absolute loader in ROM that loads the real loader | fixed in hardware |
| Relocating loader (BSS) | relocates using a relocation bit mask, links only in a limited way | one pass over the module |
| Direct-linking loader | full relocation **and** symbol resolution at load time, allows separate compilation | the general-purpose answer |
| Dynamic loading | a routine is loaded only when first called | saves memory for rarely used code |
| Dynamic linking | library symbols are bound at run time from a shared object | one library copy serves all processes |

**Static linking** copies library code into the executable: bigger files, no run-time dependency, and a library bug fix requires relinking. **Dynamic linking** leaves a stub which, on first call, locates the routine in the shared library: smaller executables, shared memory pages, and library updates take effect without relinking — but the program fails if the shared object is missing or incompatible.

items: Pass 1: initialise LC from START; for each statement, if it has a label, enter (label, LC) in SYMTAB.
Pass 1: look up the mnemonic in OPTAB to get the instruction length and advance LC; handle DS/DC/ORIGIN/EQU specially.
Pass 1: on a literal, add it to LITTAB without an address; on LTORG or END, assign consecutive addresses to the current pool and record the pool in POOLTAB.
Pass 2: re-read the intermediate code, replace each symbol with its SYMTAB address and each mnemonic with its OPTAB opcode.
Pass 2: emit the object module — text records, the entry point, the external definition and reference tables, and the relocation information.
Linker: place each module, resolve every external reference against the combined definition table, apply relocation, produce a single load module.
Loader: read the load module into memory at the allocated base, apply any remaining relocation, and jump to the entry point.

blocks.title: Counting passes the fast way
blocks.text: Ask one question: *does this tool ever need information that appears later in its input?* If yes, it needs two passes or backpatching. A two-pass **assembler** needs pass 1 only for forward references; a two-pass **macro processor** needs pass 1 only to find macro definitions. If the language requires all definitions before use, one pass is enough.

blocks.q: In a two-pass assembler, the symbol table is
opts: created in pass 1 and used in pass 2
created and used entirely in pass 1
created in pass 2 and used in pass 1
created and used entirely in pass 2
blocks.exp: Pass 1 walks the source with the location counter and records the address of every label. Pass 2 needs those addresses to generate the operand fields, so it only reads the table. This is the defining reason the assembler has two passes at all.

blocks.q: A program contains 20 invocations of a 6-instruction macro. Compared with using a 6-instruction subroutine, the macro version
opts: produces a smaller object program but runs slower
produces a larger object program but avoids call/return overhead
is identical in both size and speed
produces a larger object program and also runs slower
blocks.exp: Each invocation is expanded inline, so the macro version contributes roughly $20 \times 6 = 120$ instructions against about 6 plus 20 call sites for the subroutine. In exchange there is no call, no return and no linkage save/restore, so the macro version executes fewer instructions at run time.

tricks.title: LC arithmetic is the whole question
tricks.body: Most assembler questions reduce to running the location counter down the listing. Only `DS`, `DC`, `ORIGIN`, `START`, `LTORG` and ordinary instructions move it. `EQU` never does. If you keep a two-column tally of LC and statement you will not get these wrong.

tricks.title: Literals land at the LTORG, not where they are written
tricks.body: A literal such as `='5'` is collected when seen and given an address only at the next `LTORG` or at `END`. So a literal used at address 101 can perfectly well sit at address 105. Questions are designed so the naive answer is the address of use.

tricks.title: Macro equals size, subroutine equals time
tricks.body: Whenever a question compares them, macros trade memory for speed and subroutines trade speed for memory. Nothing else needs to be remembered to answer the comparison questions.

tricks.title: Static versus dynamic linking in one line
tricks.body: Static: everything bound before run time, bigger image, self-contained. Dynamic: binding deferred to first use, smaller image, one shared copy in memory, breaks if the library is absent. Any statement that gives dynamic linking a *larger* executable is false.

traps.title: Linking is not loading
traps.body: The linker combines modules and resolves symbol names; the loader places the resulting image in memory and starts it. A question that says the loader resolves external references is describing a *linking loader* specifically, not a loader in general. Relocation can be done by either, which is precisely why the taxonomy of loaders exists.

traps.title: Nested macro call versus nested macro definition
traps.body: A macro whose body *calls* another macro is a nested call and is handled during expansion. A macro whose body *defines* another macro creates the inner macro only when the outer one is expanded, so the inner macro does not exist in MNT until then.

traps.title: One-pass does not mean no forward references
traps.body: A one-pass assembler still handles forward references — it just resolves them by backpatching rather than by a second scan. The claim that a one-pass assembler cannot assemble forward references is false.

topics.title: Operating System Basics, Structure and Services
topics.summary: What an OS is, how kernels are structured, and how a user program crosses into the kernel.

blocks.text:
## What an operating system actually does

An operating system has two jobs that pull in opposite directions. As a **resource manager** it must keep the CPU, memory, disks and devices busy and fairly shared. As an **extended machine** it must hide the ugly reality of those devices behind clean abstractions — a process instead of a CPU, an address space instead of DRAM, a file instead of a disk block. Almost every design decision in an OS is a compromise between these two roles.

The services an OS exposes fall into a short list worth memorising: program execution, I/O operations, file-system manipulation, communication, error detection, resource allocation, accounting and protection. The first five exist for the user's benefit; the last three exist for the system's.

## Dual-mode operation

Protection rests on one hardware feature: a **mode bit** in the processor status word.

- In **user mode** a set of instructions is illegal — halting the machine, changing the memory-management registers, doing raw I/O, altering the interrupt vector. These are the **privileged instructions**.
- In **kernel mode** (also called supervisor, system or monitor mode) everything is legal.

A user program cannot simply set the mode bit; if it could, the protection would be worthless. The only way in is a **trap** — a deliberate software interrupt — which simultaneously switches to kernel mode and transfers control to a fixed address chosen by the kernel. That is the system call mechanism.

The distinction that examiners test constantly:

| Event | Source | Synchronous with the instruction stream? |
|---|---|---|
| Interrupt | external device | no — arrives at an arbitrary moment |
| Trap / exception | the executing instruction itself | yes — reproducible |
| System call | a deliberate trap issued by software | yes |

Division by zero and a page fault are traps. A timer tick or a disk-completion signal is an interrupt. A system call is a trap that the program *wanted*.

## System calls

A system call is the programming interface to the kernel. Parameters are passed in registers, in a block whose address is in a register, or on the stack. The standard categories are process control (`fork`, `exec`, `wait`, `exit`), file management (`open`, `read`, `write`, `close`), device management (`ioctl`), information maintenance (`getpid`, `time`), communication (`pipe`, `shmget`, `send`) and protection (`chmod`, `umask`).

What happens on a call such as `read(fd, buf, n)`:

1. The library wrapper places the system-call number and arguments where the ABI says.
2. It executes the trap instruction (`syscall`, `int 0x80`, `svc`).
3. The hardware switches to kernel mode and vectors to the kernel's trap handler.
4. The handler validates the arguments, indexes the system-call table and runs the service routine.
5. On return, the mode bit flips back and control resumes at the instruction after the trap.

Note what is *not* a system call: a call to `printf` or `strlen` is an ordinary library call. `printf` eventually causes a `write` system call, but the C library function itself is user-level code.

## Kernel structures

**Monolithic.** The whole kernel — scheduler, memory manager, file systems, drivers — is one program running in one address space. Calls between subsystems are plain function calls, so it is fast, but a bug anywhere can corrupt anything. Classic Unix and Linux are monolithic (Linux adds loadable modules, which does not change the address-space story).

**Layered.** The kernel is a stack of layers, each using only the layer below. Easy to reason about and debug, but deciding the order of layers is hard and every crossing costs a call, so performance suffers. THE was the textbook example.

**Microkernel.** Only the bare minimum stays in kernel mode: address spaces, threads, and inter-process communication. File systems, drivers and network stacks become ordinary user processes talking by message passing. This gives strong isolation, easier extension and better reliability — a driver crash kills one server, not the machine — at the cost of many more user/kernel crossings. Mach and QNX are the examples; macOS is a hybrid built over Mach.

**Modular.** A monolithic core with dynamically loadable modules, which is how modern Linux and Solaris are actually organised. It gives microkernel-like flexibility with monolithic-like speed, because modules are loaded into the kernel address space.

**Virtual machine.** A hypervisor presents each guest with what looks like bare hardware, so several operating systems run side by side.

**Exokernel.** The kernel only multiplexes hardware safely and lets applications implement their own abstractions in a library OS.

blocks.title: Microkernel performance
blocks.text: A microkernel is **not** faster than a monolithic kernel. Every service that used to be a function call becomes at least two context switches and two message copies. Its advantages are reliability, extensibility, portability and security. Any option that claims microkernels win on raw speed is wrong.

## Types of system

| System | Defining property | Optimises |
|---|---|---|
| Batch | jobs submitted in groups, no interaction | throughput |
| Multiprogramming | several jobs resident, CPU switches on I/O wait | CPU utilisation |
| Time sharing (multitasking) | switching fast enough for interactive use | response time |
| Real time (hard) | deadlines must be met, guaranteed | worst-case latency |
| Real time (soft) | deadlines are important but misses are tolerated | average latency |
| Distributed | independent machines cooperating over a network | scalability, sharing |
| Clustered | tightly coupled machines sharing storage | availability |

Multiprogramming and time sharing differ in intent, not mechanism: both keep several jobs in memory, but time sharing adds a timer-driven preemption so no job can hold the CPU long enough to hurt interactivity.

blocks.title: Worked example — CPU utilisation under multiprogramming
blocks.text:
Suppose each process spends a fraction $p$ of its time waiting for I/O, and $n$ processes are resident. If the waits are independent, the probability that *all* $n$ are waiting simultaneously is $p^{n}$, so

$$\text{CPU utilisation} = 1 - p^{n}$$

Take $p = 0.8$ (an I/O-bound workload).

- $n = 1$: $1 - 0.8 = 0.20$, i.e. 20%.
- $n = 2$: $1 - 0.64 = 0.36$.
- $n = 4$: $1 - 0.8^{4} = 1 - 0.4096 = 0.5904 \approx 59\%$.
- $n = 10$: $1 - 0.8^{10} = 1 - 0.1074 = 0.8926 \approx 89\%$.

How many processes are needed for at least 90% utilisation? Solve $0.8^{n} \le 0.1$, so $n \ge \log 0.1 / \log 0.8 = (-1)/(-0.0969) = 10.3$, giving $n = 11$.

The lesson the numbers teach: the gain from adding processes falls off quickly, which is why real systems reach a point where more multiprogramming buys nothing and only costs memory.

blocks.q: Which of the following is NOT a privileged instruction?
opts: Switch from user mode to kernel mode
blocks.exp: Reading the clock leaks no control and damages nothing, so it is allowed in user mode (often without even a trap, via a shared page). Setting the timer, changing the mode bit and touching another process's memory would each let a user program defeat the OS, so all three are privileged.

blocks.q: In a system where each process is I/O bound 50% of the time, the CPU utilisation with 3 processes in memory is
blocks.exp: Utilisation is $1 - p^{n}$ with $p = 0.5$ and $n = 3$, so $1 - 0.125 = 0.875$, i.e. 87.5%. Note that halving the I/O fraction matters far more than adding a fourth process.

tricks.title: Privileged or not — ask who gets hurt
tricks.body: An instruction is privileged exactly when a malicious user program could use it to break isolation or hog the machine. Timer, I/O, memory-management registers, interrupt table, mode bit: privileged. Arithmetic, reading the clock, ordinary loads and stores: not.

tricks.title: $1-p^n$ is the only formula in this topic
tricks.body: Every multiprogramming utilisation question is $1-p^{n}$ with $p$ the I/O-wait fraction. If the question gives 'CPU burst fraction' instead, remember that $p$ is the *waiting* fraction, so convert first.

tricks.title: Read the structure question backwards
tricks.body: Options describing reliability, extensibility, isolation or a driver crash not killing the system point to microkernel. Options describing speed and direct function calls point to monolithic. Options about ordering constraints and debugging ease point to layered.

traps.title: Library call versus system call
traps.body: `fopen` is a C library function; `open` is a system call. `malloc` is a library function that sometimes calls `brk`/`mmap`. Questions list a mixture and ask which are system calls — the test is whether the kernel must be entered.

traps.title: Multiprogramming does not require time sharing
traps.body: Multiprogramming only needs a way to switch on I/O wait. Time sharing additionally requires a timer interrupt so that a compute-bound process is preempted. Every time-sharing system is multiprogrammed; the converse is false.

topics.title: Process Management and Interprocess Communication
topics.summary: Process states, the PCB, context switching, fork semantics and the two IPC models.

blocks.text:
## A process is a program in motion

A program is a passive file on disk. A **process** is that program plus everything needed to keep it running: the current value of the program counter, the registers, the stack, the heap, the open files, the accounting information. Two processes can run the same program and remain completely independent, because each has its own copy of this state.

The address space of a process has four classic regions:

| Region | Contents | Grows |
|---|---|---|
| Text | machine instructions | fixed |
| Data | initialised and uninitialised globals | fixed at load, extended by `brk` |
| Heap | dynamically allocated memory | upward |
| Stack | activation records, locals, return addresses | downward |

Heap and stack grow toward each other so that the unused gap between them serves both.

## The process state diagram

The five-state model:

- **New** — the process is being created.
- **Ready** — it could run, it just does not have a CPU.
- **Running** — it is on a CPU right now.
- **Waiting (blocked)** — it cannot proceed until an event happens, typically I/O completion.
- **Terminated** — it has finished.

The legal transitions are the part that gets examined:

| Transition | Cause |
|---|---|
| Ready $\to$ Running | the scheduler dispatches it |
| Running $\to$ Ready | **preemption** — the quantum expired or a higher-priority process arrived |
| Running $\to$ Waiting | it issued a blocking request (I/O, `wait`, semaphore `P`) |
| Waiting $\to$ Ready | the event occurred |
| Running $\to$ Terminated | `exit` or a fatal error |

There is **no** Waiting $\to$ Running transition and **no** Ready $\to$ Waiting transition. A blocked process must pass through Ready, and a ready process cannot block because it is not executing and therefore cannot issue a request. Those two impossible arrows are the single most common trap in this topic.

Adding swapping gives two more states, **ready-suspended** and **blocked-suspended**, for processes whose images have been moved out to backing store.

## The process control block

The PCB is the kernel's record of a process. It holds the process id, the current state, the program counter and saved registers, scheduling information (priority, queue pointers), memory-management information (page-table base or segment table, limits), accounting data (CPU used, time limits), and the I/O status (open-file table, pending devices).

A **context switch** is exactly: save the running process's CPU state into its PCB, update its state field, pick another process, restore that process's state from its PCB, and, if the new process is in a different address space, reload the memory-management registers and flush or tag the TLB.

Context switching is **pure overhead** — the machine does no useful work during it. Its cost is why quantum selection matters in round robin and why threads, which share an address space and therefore avoid the TLB and page-table work, switch far faster than processes.

## Process creation: fork and exec

In Unix, `fork()` creates a child that is a copy of the parent. It returns **twice**: 0 in the child and the child's pid in the parent (or $-1$ on failure). The child gets a copy of the address space — in practice a copy-on-write copy, so the pages are shared read-only until one side writes.

`exec()` replaces the current image with a new program; it does **not** create a process, and on success it never returns. The idiom is `fork` then `exec` in the child, `wait` in the parent.

Counting processes created by nested forks is a standard numerical. After $n$ successive `fork()` calls executed unconditionally, the number of processes is $2^{n}$, so the number of **new** processes created is $2^{n}-1$.

Two terminology items:

- A **zombie** has terminated but its parent has not yet called `wait`, so the exit status is still held in the process table.
- An **orphan** is still running but its parent has died; it is re-parented to `init` (pid 1), which reaps it.

blocks.text:
## Interprocess communication

Processes are isolated by design, so the OS must supply explicit channels. There are exactly two models.

**Shared memory.** The kernel sets up a region mapped into two or more address spaces (`shmget`, `shmat`). After setup the kernel is out of the way, so transfer is at memory speed — this is the **faster** model for bulk data. The cost is that all synchronisation is the programmer's responsibility; nothing stops two processes writing the same word.

**Message passing.** Processes exchange discrete messages through `send` and `receive` primitives implemented by the kernel. Every message costs at least two copies and two kernel crossings, so it is slower for large volumes, but it needs no shared address space and therefore works unchanged across machines, which is why distributed systems use it.

Design choices within message passing:

| Choice | Options |
|---|---|
| Naming | direct (name the process) vs indirect (name a mailbox/port) |
| Synchronisation | blocking (synchronous) vs non-blocking (asynchronous) send/receive |
| Buffering | zero capacity (rendezvous), bounded, unbounded |

A **zero-capacity** link forces the sender to block until the receiver takes the message — that is a rendezvous. With **unbounded** capacity the sender never blocks.

Unix-level mechanisms: **pipes** (unidirectional, related processes, byte stream, `|`), **named pipes / FIFOs** (unrelated processes, persist in the file system), **message queues**, **shared memory segments**, **sockets** (across machines) and **signals** (asynchronous notification, not a data channel).

blocks.q: Which process state transition is impossible?
blocks.exp: A process in the Ready state is not executing, so it cannot issue the blocking request that would move it to Waiting. It must first be dispatched to Running. The other three are the normal preemption, event-completion and I/O-request transitions.

blocks.q: A process executes `fork(); fork(); fork();` unconditionally. The number of child processes created is
blocks.exp: The total number of processes after $n$ forks is $2^{n} = 8$, but one of those is the original parent, so the number of *children* created is $2^{3}-1 = 7$. Read whether the question asks for total processes or new ones — the two answers 8 and 7 are both offered on purpose.

tricks.title: Fork counting is powers of two, minus traps
tricks.body: Unconditional forks: $n$ forks give $2^{n}$ processes and $2^{n}-1$ children. The only complications are short-circuit operators (`&&`, `||`), forks inside loops (a loop of $n$ iterations behaves like $n$ sequential forks, so still $2^n$), and forks guarded by a test on the return value.

tricks.title: Printf line counting with buffering
tricks.body: If a question prints *before* forking without a newline, the buffered text is duplicated into every child, so the count can exceed the naive number. With a trailing `\n` on a terminal the buffer is flushed and each process prints once.

tricks.title: Shared memory fast, message passing portable
tricks.body: Any comparison question resolves the same way: shared memory wins on speed inside one machine, message passing wins on simplicity of synchronisation and works across machines.

traps.title: exec does not create a process
traps.body: `fork` creates, `exec` replaces. A successful `exec` never returns, and the process id is unchanged. An option saying `exec` spawns a new process is always wrong.

traps.title: Zombie versus orphan
traps.body: Zombie: child dead, parent alive but not reaping. Orphan: child alive, parent dead. The zombie occupies a process-table slot but no memory; the orphan is adopted by `init`.

traps.title: Context switch is not the same as mode switch
traps.body: Entering the kernel for a system call is a mode switch and does not change which process is running. A context switch changes the running process and is strictly more expensive.

topics.title: Process Synchronization
topics.summary: The critical-section problem, Peterson's solution, hardware primitives, semaphores, monitors and the classic problems.

blocks.text:
## Why synchronisation is needed

When two processes share data, the result can depend on the interleaving of their instructions. That is a **race condition**. The standard illustration is a shared counter:

```
P1: reg1 = count;  reg1 = reg1 + 1;  count = reg1;
P2: reg2 = count;  reg2 = reg2 - 1;  count = reg2;
```

Starting from `count = 5`, a sequential execution in either order leaves 5. But the interleaving `reg1 = count; reg2 = count; reg1 = reg1+1; count = reg1; reg2 = reg2-1; count = reg2` leaves 4, and the mirror interleaving leaves 6. Nothing is wrong with either process in isolation; the bug lives in the interleaving.

The section of code that touches the shared data is the **critical section**. Any correct solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three properties:

1. **Mutual exclusion** — at most one process is in its critical section at a time.
2. **Progress** — if no process is in its critical section and some want to enter, only the contending processes participate in the decision, and the decision cannot be postponed indefinitely.
3. **Bounded waiting** — there is a limit on how many times other processes may enter after a process has made its request and before that request is granted.

Progress rules out deadlock; bounded waiting rules out starvation. Mutual exclusion alone is easy — an algorithm that lets nobody in satisfies it.

## Peterson's solution

Peterson's algorithm solves the problem for **two processes** using only ordinary loads and stores. The shared variables are `boolean flag[2]`, initially both false, and `int turn`.

```c
/* process i, the other is j = 1 - i */
flag[i] = true;          /* I want to enter            */
turn = j;                 /* but you may go first       */
while (flag[j] && turn == j)
    ;                     /* busy wait                  */

/* --- critical section --- */

flag[i] = false;          /* I am done                  */
```

Why it works:

- **Mutual exclusion.** For both to be inside, both loops must have exited, so for $P_0$ either `flag[1]` was false or `turn` was 0, and symmetrically for $P_1$. If both set their flags, the only remaining escape is `turn`, and `turn` holds a single value. Both processes write `turn` but the **last write wins**, and exactly one of them is last, so exactly one is released.
- **Progress.** If $P_1$ is not interested, `flag[1]` is false and $P_0$ walks straight in. The decision never involves a process sitting in its remainder section.
- **Bounded waiting.** The bound is one: after $P_0$ exits and immediately wants to re-enter, it sets `turn = 1`, which lets $P_1$ in first. Neither process can enter twice while the other waits.

The order of the two assignments matters absolutely. Setting `turn = j` *before* `flag[i] = true` breaks mutual exclusion. Swapping to `turn = i` breaks it too — the polite gesture of giving the turn away is the whole idea.

blocks.title: What Peterson's solution does not do
blocks.text: It handles **exactly two** processes; the $n$-process generalisations are the bakery algorithm and the tournament construction. It uses **busy waiting**, so it burns CPU (a spinlock, not a blocking lock). And it assumes loads and stores are not reordered — on a modern out-of-order processor it needs memory fences to be correct, which is why textbooks present it as a teaching device rather than as production code.

## Monitors

A **monitor** is a language construct: a module whose procedures are guaranteed to execute with mutual exclusion, so the compiler, not the programmer, inserts the locking. Inside it, **condition variables** provide waiting, with operations `wait(c)` (release the monitor and sleep) and `signal(c)` (wake one waiter, or do nothing if none is waiting).

The key difference from a semaphore: a `signal` on a condition variable with no waiter is **lost**, whereas `signal` on a semaphore increments a counter and is remembered. That asymmetry is a favourite question.

Two signalling disciplines:

- **Hoare (signal-and-wait)** — the signaller yields the monitor immediately to the woken process, so the condition is guaranteed true on wake-up. Written with `if`.
- **Mesa (signal-and-continue)** — the signaller keeps running and the woken process must re-check, because another process may have intervened. Written with `while`. Java and real systems use Mesa semantics, which is why you always write `while (!condition) wait();`.

blocks.title: Worked example — tracing a counting semaphore
blocks.text:
A counting semaphore `S` is initialised to 3. Ten processes each execute `wait(S)`, then their critical section, and five of them later execute `signal(S)`. Take a snapshot **after all ten waits have been attempted and the five signals have completed**.

Apply the invariant $S = S_{\text{init}} - W + V$ where $W$ is the number of `wait` operations attempted and $V$ the number of signals:

$$S = 3 - 10 + 5 = -2$$

So the semaphore's value is $-2$, and $|-2| = 2$ processes are blocked on its queue.

Check this against the story. The first three waits succeed ($S$: 3, 2, 1, 0). The next seven block ($S$: $-1 \ldots -7$). Each of the five signals raises $S$ by one and releases one blocked process ($S$: $-6, -5, -4, -3, -2$), so 5 of the 7 blocked processes have been released and $7 - 5 = 2$ remain blocked. Both routes agree.

Now a variant that changes the answer. If the implementation never lets $S$ go below 0 (the value-stays-non-negative style), the final value would be $\max(0, 3-10+5) = 0$ and the blocked count would have to be tracked separately. Read the definition the question gives you before applying the formula.

blocks.q: In Peterson's solution, process $P_i$ executes `flag[i] = true; turn = j;`. If the two statements are interchanged, which property is violated?
blocks.exp: With `turn = j` first, $P_0$ can set `turn = 1` and be preempted before setting `flag[0]`. Then $P_1$ sets `turn = 0`, sets `flag[1]`, sees `flag[0]` still false and enters. $P_0$ resumes, sets `flag[0] = true`, finds `turn == 0`, and enters as well. Both are inside, so mutual exclusion fails.

blocks.q: A binary semaphore `mutex` is initialised to 1. In the producer-consumer solution a programmer writes `wait(mutex); wait(empty);` in the producer. The consequence is
opts: nothing; the order of waits is irrelevant
deadlock when the buffer is full
the mutual exclusion property is lost
blocks.exp: If the buffer is full, `empty` is 0, so the producer blocks on `wait(empty)` while still holding `mutex`. The consumer then blocks on `wait(mutex)` and can never remove an item, so `empty` never rises. Neither can proceed, which is a classic deadlock — always take the counting semaphore before the mutex.

tricks.title: Semaphore value in one line
tricks.body: $S = S_{\text{init}} - (\#\text{wait}) + (\#\text{signal})$, and if the result is negative its magnitude is the number of blocked processes. This answers almost every semaphore numerical in a single step.

tricks.title: Mutex innermost, counters outermost
tricks.body: In any producer-consumer style code the correct nesting is: counting semaphore first, mutex second, and release in the reverse order. If a question shows the mutex acquired first, the answer is deadlock.

tricks.title: Peterson's bound is exactly one
tricks.body: When asked for the bounded-waiting bound of Peterson's solution the answer is 1: the other process can enter at most once ahead of you. Do not answer $n-1$ — that is the bakery algorithm.

tricks.title: Symmetry breaking fixes dining philosophers
tricks.body: Any fix that destroys the circular symmetry works: limit to $n-1$ diners, reverse the pick-up order for one philosopher, or grab both forks atomically. If an option preserves perfect symmetry with left-then-right, it still deadlocks.

traps.title: A lost signal on a condition variable
traps.body: `signal` on a semaphore is remembered because it increments the count. `signal` on a monitor condition variable with no one waiting is discarded. Questions exploit the assumption that the two behave alike.

traps.title: Busy waiting versus blocking
traps.body: Peterson's solution, test-and-set loops and spinlocks all busy-wait. Semaphores and monitors block. Saying that a semaphore solution eliminates busy waiting entirely is slightly generous — the internal `wait`/`signal` may spin for a few instructions — but at the exam's level of abstraction, semaphore equals blocking.

traps.title: Mutual exclusion alone is not correctness
traps.body: An algorithm that strictly alternates using only `turn` gives mutual exclusion and bounded waiting but fails **progress**: if $P_0$ never wants to enter again, $P_1$ can never enter a second time. This is the standard 'Algorithm 1' counterexample.

topics.title: Threads and Multicore Programming
topics.summary: Threads versus processes, user- and kernel-level models, thread pools, and Amdahl's law on multicore hardware.

blocks.text:
## What a thread is

A process bundles two things: a **resource container** (address space, open files, accounting) and a **unit of execution** (program counter, registers, stack). A thread separates the second from the first. Several threads can live inside one process, each with its own program counter, register set and stack, while sharing the code, the data segment, the heap and the open-file table.

The practical consequences follow directly from what is shared:

| Item | Per thread | Shared by all threads of a process |
|---|---|---|
| Program counter, registers | yes | — |
| Stack | yes | — |
| Thread id, priority, signal mask, errno | yes | — |
| Code (text) segment | — | yes |
| Global and static data | — | yes |
| Heap | — | yes |
| Open files, working directory, user id | — | yes |

Because globals and the heap are shared, threads communicate with no kernel help at all — but for the same reason they need synchronisation for everything, and one thread's stray pointer can corrupt another's data. Processes pay for isolation with the cost of IPC; threads buy speed by giving up isolation.

## Why threads are cheap

Creating a thread does not require building an address space, a page table or a file-descriptor table. Switching between two threads **of the same process** does not require reloading the memory-management registers and does not invalidate the TLB, so the cost is roughly the cost of saving and restoring registers. Switching between threads of *different* processes is a full context switch and saves nothing.

The four standard benefits: **responsiveness** (one thread blocks, the interface keeps running), **resource sharing** (free, by construction), **economy** (cheaper to create and switch than processes), and **scalability** (threads can run on different cores simultaneously, a single-threaded process cannot).

## User-level and kernel-level threads

**User-level threads** are managed by a library in user space. The kernel sees one process and knows nothing about the threads. Creation and switching are fast function calls with no system call at all. The fatal weakness: if one thread makes a blocking system call, the kernel blocks the whole process, so every thread stops. Also, the process gets one CPU, so user threads cannot exploit multiple cores.

**Kernel-level threads** are scheduled by the kernel itself. A blocking call blocks only the calling thread, and different threads can run on different cores. The cost is that every create, destroy and switch is a system call.

The mapping between them gives the standard models:

| Model | Description | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Many-to-one | many user threads onto one kernel thread | one blocking call stops all; no true parallelism |
| One-to-one | each user thread gets its own kernel thread | true parallelism; kernel-thread count must be capped (Linux, Windows) |
| Many-to-many | $m$ user threads multiplexed onto $n \le m$ kernel threads | most flexible, hardest to implement |
| Two-level | many-to-many plus the option to bind one user thread to one kernel thread | combines both |

**Scheduler activations** are the mechanism that makes many-to-many work: the kernel gives the user-level library an **upcall** when a thread blocks or a processor becomes available, so the library can reschedule its remaining threads.

blocks.title: Implicit threading
blocks.text: Writing explicit threads is error-prone, so modern systems hide them. A **thread pool** creates a fixed number of workers at start-up and hands them tasks from a queue: it bounds the number of threads, removes creation cost from the critical path, and decouples task submission from execution. **OpenMP** marks parallel regions with compiler directives; **Grand Central Dispatch** and fork-join frameworks push tasks to a runtime. The exam angle is simply: *why a thread pool?* — bounded concurrency plus no per-task creation cost.

## Threading issues

- **fork and exec.** If a multithreaded process calls `fork`, some systems duplicate only the calling thread and some duplicate all of them. If an `exec` follows immediately, duplicating only the caller is correct and far cheaper.
- **Signal handling.** A synchronous signal (illegal instruction, divide by zero) goes to the thread that caused it. An asynchronous signal (Ctrl-C) may be delivered to one thread, to every thread, to a designated thread, or to a dedicated signal-handling thread, depending on the system.
- **Thread cancellation.** *Asynchronous* cancellation kills the target at once and may leave shared data inconsistent or resources leaked. *Deferred* cancellation sets a flag and the target terminates at a **cancellation point** where it is safe. Deferred is the default and the safe answer.
- **Thread-local storage (TLS)** gives each thread a private copy of a named variable — distinct from a local variable, which vanishes on return, because TLS persists across function calls for the life of the thread.

## Concurrency, parallelism and the limits of multicore

**Concurrency** means more than one task is in progress; it can be achieved on a single core by interleaving. **Parallelism** means more than one task is *executing at the same instant* and needs more than one core. Concurrency is a program structure; parallelism is a hardware outcome.

**Data parallelism** splits the same operation across a partitioned data set (each core sums a slice of the array). **Task parallelism** gives different cores different operations on possibly the same data.

The ceiling on what parallelism can buy is **Amdahl's law**. If a fraction $S$ of the work is inherently serial and the remaining $1-S$ parallelises perfectly over $N$ cores, then

$$\text{Speedup} \le \frac{1}{S + \dfrac{1-S}{N}}$$

As $N \to \infty$ this tends to $1/S$, so a program that is 10% serial can never run more than 10 times faster no matter how many cores it is given.

blocks.title: Worked example — Amdahl's law with real numbers
blocks.text:
An application spends 25% of its time in a strictly serial phase; the remaining 75% parallelises perfectly. Compute the speedup on 2, 4 and 8 cores, and the limit.

With $S = 0.25$:

- $N = 2$: $\dfrac{1}{0.25 + 0.75/2} = \dfrac{1}{0.25 + 0.375} = \dfrac{1}{0.625} = 1.6$
- $N = 4$: $\dfrac{1}{0.25 + 0.1875} = \dfrac{1}{0.4375} = 2.286$
- $N = 8$: $\dfrac{1}{0.25 + 0.09375} = \dfrac{1}{0.34375} = 2.909$
- $N \to \infty$: $\dfrac{1}{0.25} = 4$

So quadrupling the cores from 2 to 8 improves the speedup only from 1.6 to 2.9, and even infinite hardware caps at 4.

The reverse question is common too. *How many cores are needed for a speedup of 3?* Solve $\dfrac{1}{0.25 + 0.75/N} = 3$, so $0.25 + 0.75/N = 1/3$, giving $0.75/N = 0.08\overline{3}$ and $N = 9$. Nine cores for a speedup of three — the arithmetic is the argument against assuming that more cores fix slow programs.

blocks.q: Which of the following is NOT shared between threads of the same process?
blocks.exp: Each thread needs its own call chain, so each has a private stack (and private registers and program counter). Code, globals, heap and the file-descriptor table all belong to the process and are shared.

blocks.q: A program is 40% serial. The maximum speedup achievable with an unlimited number of processors is
blocks.exp: As $N \to \infty$ the parallel term $(1-S)/N$ vanishes, so the speedup tends to $1/S = 1/0.4 = 2.5$. The serial fraction, not the core count, is the binding constraint.

tricks.title: Amdahl's limit is just $1/S$
tricks.body: If a question asks for the maximum possible speedup with unlimited processors, do not build the full formula — answer $1/S$ where $S$ is the serial fraction. Only when a finite $N$ is given do you need the denominator $S + (1-S)/N$.

tricks.title: Decide sharing by asking 'does it belong to the address space?'
tricks.body: Anything that is part of the address space or the process's kernel bookkeeping (text, data, heap, files, uid, cwd) is shared. Anything needed to describe where a single flow of control currently is (PC, registers, stack, signal mask, errno) is private.

tricks.title: Many-to-one fails on the blocking test
tricks.body: Any question that mentions one thread issuing a blocking system call and the whole process stalling is describing user-level threads, that is, the many-to-one model. Any question about running on multiple cores rules many-to-one out.

traps.title: Concurrency is not parallelism
traps.body: A single-core machine can be concurrent but never parallel. Statements like 'multithreading requires a multicore processor' are false — multithreading predates multicore and is still useful for responsiveness and overlapping I/O.

traps.title: Thread switch is not always cheap
traps.body: Switching between threads of *different* processes costs exactly as much as a process context switch, because the address space still changes. The saving applies only within a process.

traps.title: User-level threads are fast to switch but cannot use two cores
traps.body: Both halves matter. Options that credit user-level threads with parallel execution across processors are wrong; options that credit them with low switching cost are right.

topics.title: CPU Scheduling
topics.summary: Scheduling criteria and every algorithm from FCFS to multilevel feedback, with the convoy and starvation behaviour that questions turn on.

blocks.text:
## The problem and the vocabulary

Multiprogramming exists so that the CPU is never idle while a process waits for I/O. The **short-term scheduler** picks, from the ready queue, which process runs next; the **dispatcher** performs the switch, and the time it takes is the **dispatch latency**.

Four times matter for each process:

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| Arrival time $AT$ | when the process enters the ready queue |
| Burst time $BT$ | CPU time it needs |
| Completion time $CT$ | when it finishes |
| **Turnaround time** | $TAT = CT - AT$ |
| **Waiting time** | $WT = TAT - BT$ |
| **Response time** | first time it gets the CPU, minus $AT$ |

Those two derived identities are all the arithmetic you need. Turnaround is total time in the system; waiting is the part of it spent not executing; response is how long until the user sees *something*, which is why interactive systems optimise it separately.

Scheduling is **non-preemptive** if a process keeps the CPU until it blocks or exits, and **preemptive** if the kernel can take the CPU away — on quantum expiry, or when a better candidate arrives. Preemption requires a timer and makes shared-data protection necessary inside the kernel, which is the price it pays.

## First-come first-served (FCFS)

The ready queue is FIFO. FCFS is non-preemptive, trivially fair in the sense that nobody is overtaken, and free of starvation.

Its fatal flaw is the **convoy effect**. One long CPU-bound process at the head of the queue holds the CPU while every short I/O-bound process queues behind it. When the long process finally blocks, the short ones run briefly, all rush to the I/O device, and the long process gets the CPU back — so the devices idle while the CPU is busy and the CPU idles while the devices are busy. Average waiting time is high and, worse, it depends violently on arrival order: the same three processes with burst times 24, 3, 3 give an average wait of 17 in that order and 3 in the order 3, 3, 24.

## Shortest job first and shortest remaining time first

**SJF** picks the ready process with the smallest next CPU burst. It is **provably optimal** for average waiting time among non-preemptive schedules: exchanging any adjacent pair so the shorter runs first cannot increase the total wait. **SRTF** is the preemptive version — on each arrival, if the newcomer's burst is shorter than the running process's *remaining* time, preempt. SRTF gives the minimum possible average waiting time for a given set of arrivals and bursts.

The problem is that the next burst length is not known. It is **predicted** by exponential averaging:

$$\tau_{n+1} = \alpha\, t_n + (1-\alpha)\, \tau_n$$

where $t_n$ is the length of the burst that just ended and $\tau_n$ was the prediction for it. $\alpha = 0$ ignores history's most recent value entirely and keeps the initial estimate forever; $\alpha = 1$ ignores all history except the last burst; $\alpha = 0.5$ is the usual choice, weighting the past geometrically.

Both SJF and SRTF **starve** long processes: while short jobs keep arriving, a long job never reaches the front.

blocks.title: Worked example — four processes under four algorithms
blocks.text:
| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| $P_1$ | 0 | 8 |
| $P_2$ | 1 | 4 |
| $P_3$ | 2 | 9 |
| $P_4$ | 3 | 5 |

**FCFS.** Order $P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4$: intervals 0–8, 8–12, 12–21, 21–26.
$TAT = 8, 11, 19, 23$ (sum 61, average **15.25**). $WT = 0, 7, 10, 18$ (sum 35, average **8.75**).

**SJF (non-preemptive).** At $t=0$ only $P_1$ is present so it runs 0–8. At $t=8$ the candidates are $P_2(4), P_3(9), P_4(5)$, so $P_2$ runs 8–12, then $P_4$ 12–17, then $P_3$ 17–26.
$CT = 8, 12, 26, 17$; $TAT = 8, 11, 24, 14$ (average **14.25**); $WT = 0, 7, 15, 9$ (average **7.75**).

**SRTF (preemptive).** $P_1$ starts. At $t=1$, $P_2$ needs 4 against $P_1$'s remaining 7, so $P_2$ preempts and runs 1–5. $P_3$ (9) and $P_4$ (5) arrive but do not beat $P_2$'s remaining time. At $t=5$ the remaining times are $P_1{:}\,7$, $P_3{:}\,9$, $P_4{:}\,5$, so $P_4$ runs 5–10, then $P_1$ 10–17, then $P_3$ 17–26.
$CT = 17, 5, 26, 10$; $TAT = 17, 4, 24, 7$ (average **13.0**); $WT = 9, 0, 15, 2$ (average **6.5**).

**Round robin, $q = 4$.** Queue evolution: $P_1$ 0–4 (remaining 4, requeued behind $P_2,P_3,P_4$), $P_2$ 4–8 (done), $P_3$ 8–12 (remaining 5), $P_4$ 12–16 (remaining 1), $P_1$ 16–20 (done), $P_3$ 20–24 (remaining 1), $P_4$ 24–25 (done), $P_3$ 25–26 (done).
$CT = 20, 8, 26, 25$; $TAT = 20, 7, 24, 22$ (average **18.25**); $WT = 12, 3, 15, 17$ (average **11.75**).

| Algorithm | Average $WT$ | Average $TAT$ |
|---|---|---|
| FCFS | 8.75 | 15.25 |
| SJF | 7.75 | 14.25 |
| **SRTF** | **6.50** | **13.00** |
| RR ($q=4$) | 11.75 | 18.25 |

SRTF wins on average waiting time, as the optimality proof guarantees. Round robin is worst on average waiting — its purpose is *response* time, and its response times here (0, 3, 6, 9) are the best of the four.

## Round robin and the quantum

Round robin is FCFS with preemption after a fixed **time quantum** $q$. It is starvation-free, and in a system with $n$ ready processes and context-switch cost $s$, no process waits more than $(n-1)(q+s)$ before running again — that bound is the reason RR is the standard interactive algorithm.

The quantum is the whole design:

- $q \to \infty$ (larger than every burst): round robin **degenerates to FCFS**.
- $q \to 0$: response time is excellent in theory, but every switch costs $s$, so the fraction of useful work is $q/(q+s)$ and the machine spends nearly all its time switching. This is *processor sharing*.
- The practical rule is that $q$ should be large enough that roughly 80% of CPU bursts finish within one quantum, typically 10–100 ms against a switch cost of microseconds.

Note that shrinking $q$ does not always reduce average turnaround time; it often increases it, because processes finish later when they are chopped into more pieces.

## Priority, ageing and highest response ratio next

**Priority scheduling** runs the highest-priority ready process; SJF is priority scheduling with priority $= 1/\text{burst}$. Priorities may be internal (computed from measured behaviour) or external (set by policy), and the scheme may be preemptive or not. Its defect is **indefinite blocking (starvation)** of low-priority processes, and the standard remedy is **ageing**: increase a process's priority the longer it waits.

**Highest response ratio next (HRRN)** is a non-preemptive scheme designed to get SJF-like behaviour without starvation. At each decision point it computes, for every ready process,

$$\text{Response ratio} = \frac{W + S}{S}$$

where $W$ is the time already spent waiting and $S$ is the estimated service time, and runs the largest. A short job starts with a high ratio, but a long job's ratio grows without bound as it waits, so it eventually wins — starvation is impossible by construction.

## Multilevel queues and multilevel feedback queues

A **multilevel queue** partitions the ready queue permanently: system processes, interactive processes, batch processes, each with its own algorithm (say RR for interactive, FCFS for batch). Scheduling *between* queues is either strict priority (which starves the low queues) or a time slice split among them (say 80% to foreground, 20% to background). A process never changes queue.

A **multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ)** allows movement. A new process enters the top queue with a small quantum; if it uses the whole quantum it is demoted to a longer-quantum, lower-priority queue. Short and interactive processes stay near the top and get fast response; CPU-bound processes sink to the bottom and get long, efficient slices. Periodic promotion of everything back to the top queue implements ageing and prevents starvation. MLFQ is the most general scheduler — it is defined by the number of queues, each queue's algorithm, the promotion rule, the demotion rule, and the rule for which queue a new process enters — and it *approximates SJF without knowing burst lengths*, which is why real systems use it.

blocks.title: Real-time scheduling bounds
blocks.text:
For $n$ periodic tasks with execution time $C_i$ and period $T_i$, the total utilisation is $U = \sum C_i / T_i$.

- **Rate monotonic** (static priority, shorter period gets higher priority) is guaranteed to schedule the set if $U \le n(2^{1/n} - 1)$. That bound is 1.0 for $n=1$, 0.828 for $n=2$, 0.780 for $n=3$, and tends to $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$. The condition is **sufficient, not necessary** — sets above the bound may still be schedulable.
- **Earliest deadline first** (dynamic priority, nearest deadline wins) succeeds if and only if $U \le 1$, so EDF is optimal for uniprocessors.

Rate monotonic is the optimal *static*-priority algorithm; EDF beats it because it may reorder priorities at run time.

blocks.title: Try it — run the algorithms yourself
blocks.note: Enter arrival and burst times and compare FCFS, SJF, SRTF, priority and round robin Gantt charts side by side.

blocks.q: Round robin scheduling with a time quantum larger than the largest CPU burst behaves identically to
blocks.exp: If no process is ever preempted, the ready queue is served strictly in arrival order, which is exactly FCFS. This is also why very large quanta destroy the responsiveness that round robin exists to provide.

blocks.q: Processes with burst times 6, 8, 7 and 3 arrive together at time 0. The average waiting time under SJF is
blocks.exp: SJF runs them in the order 3, 6, 7, 8. Start times are 0, 3, 9 and 16, so the waiting times are 0, 3, 9 and 16, summing to 28 and averaging $28/4 = 7$. With all arrivals at 0, the waiting time of the $k$th process is simply the sum of the $k-1$ bursts before it.

tricks.title: All arrivals at time 0 makes it a prefix-sum problem
tricks.body: Sort the bursts, then each process's waiting time is the running total of the ones before it. Average waiting time $=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}(n-k)\,b_k$ with $b_k$ sorted ascending — you never need a Gantt chart for this case.

tricks.title: Only compute completion times
tricks.body: Draw the Gantt chart once, read off $CT$ for each process, then apply $TAT = CT - AT$ and $WT = TAT - BT$. Trying to accumulate waiting time interval by interval is where errors creep in, especially under preemption.

tricks.title: SRTF only needs checking at arrival instants
tricks.body: A preemption decision in SRTF can only be triggered when a new process arrives or the running one finishes. So you only have to compare remaining times at those few instants, not at every tick.

tricks.title: Rank the algorithms before computing
tricks.body: For the same workload, average waiting time satisfies SRTF $\le$ SJF $\le$ FCFS, and round robin is usually the worst on waiting time but the best on response time. If your computed numbers violate that ordering, you have made an arithmetic slip.

traps.title: Waiting time under preemption
traps.body: $WT = TAT - BT$ always holds, even when a process is preempted several times, because the time it actually executed still totals $BT$. Students often try to add up idle intervals by hand and miscount the last one.

traps.title: SJF is optimal, but only for average waiting time
traps.body: SJF minimises average waiting (and hence average turnaround) time. It does not minimise response time, does not minimise the maximum waiting time, and is not fair. An option claiming SJF is optimal 'in all respects' is wrong.

traps.title: Starvation is impossible in FCFS and round robin
traps.body: Both serve every process in bounded time. Starvation belongs to SJF, SRTF, priority without ageing, and strict-priority multilevel queues. HRRN and MLFQ with periodic promotion are explicitly designed to avoid it.

topics.summary: Necessary conditions, resource-allocation graphs, the Banker's algorithm, detection, and the deadlock-free resource count.

blocks.text:
## What a deadlock is

A set of processes is **deadlocked** when every process in the set is waiting for an event that only another process in the same set can cause. Because none of them will ever run again, none of the events will ever happen. The events in question are normally resource releases.

Deadlock requires all four of the following to hold **simultaneously** — they are *necessary* conditions, and for a single-instance resource system they are also sufficient:

1. **Mutual exclusion** — at least one resource is non-sharable; only one process may use it at a time.
2. **Hold and wait** — a process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire more.
3. **No preemption** — a resource can be released only voluntarily by the process holding it.
4. **Circular wait** — there is a cycle $P_0 \to P_1 \to \cdots \to P_n \to P_0$ in which each process waits for a resource held by the next.

Break any single one and deadlock becomes impossible. Note that circular wait implies hold and wait, so the four are not independent — a fact that appears in questions asking which condition is 'not independent of the others'.

## Resource-allocation graphs

Draw processes as circles and resource types as boxes containing one dot per instance. A **request edge** goes $P_i \to R_j$; an **assignment edge** goes from a dot of $R_j$ to $P_i$.

The reading rule is precise and often mis-stated:

- **No cycle $\Rightarrow$ no deadlock**, always.
- **Cycle present and every resource type has exactly one instance $\Rightarrow$ deadlock**.
- **Cycle present with multiple instances $\Rightarrow$ deadlock is possible but not certain.** A process outside the cycle may release an instance and break it.

So a cycle is necessary for deadlock but sufficient only in the single-instance case.

## The four strategies

| Strategy | Idea | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Prevention** | structurally deny one of the four conditions | low device utilisation, starvation |
| **Avoidance** | grant a request only if the resulting state is safe | needs advance knowledge of maximum claims |
| **Detection and recovery** | let deadlocks happen, find them, break them | detection runs cost CPU; recovery loses work |
| **Ignore (ostrich)** | assume they are rare | what Unix and Windows actually do |

**Prevention** in detail. Mutual exclusion cannot generally be removed — a printer is a printer — though spooling makes sharable copies. Hold and wait is denied by requiring a process to request everything at once, or to hold nothing when it requests; both waste resources and can starve a process that needs a popular set. No preemption is denied by taking resources away from a waiting process and restarting it later, which works for CPU registers and memory but not for a half-written tape. Circular wait is denied by imposing a **total order** on resource types and insisting that requests be made in increasing order — this is the cheapest and most used prevention technique, and the one to name if a question asks for a practical one.

## Safe states and the Banker's algorithm

A state is **safe** if there exists an ordering of all processes — a **safe sequence** — such that each process can obtain its maximum remaining need from the currently available resources plus everything held by the processes before it in the sequence. A safe state is never deadlocked. An unsafe state is **not** necessarily deadlocked; it merely means the system can no longer guarantee that it will escape. The containment is:

$$\text{deadlocked} \subset \text{unsafe} \subset \text{all states}, \qquad \text{safe} \cap \text{unsafe} = \varnothing$$

The **Banker's algorithm** keeps the system in safe states. Each process declares its `Max` claim in advance. The data structures, for $n$ processes and $m$ resource types, are `Available[m]`, `Max[n][m]`, `Allocation[n][m]` and

$$\text{Need}[i][j] = \text{Max}[i][j] - \text{Allocation}[i][j]$$

On a request $\text{Request}_i$ the algorithm does three things: reject it as an error if $\text{Request}_i > \text{Need}_i$; make the process wait if $\text{Request}_i > \text{Available}$; otherwise *pretend* to allocate and run the **safety algorithm**. If the pretended state is safe, commit; if not, roll back and make the process wait.

The safety algorithm itself: set `Work = Available` and `Finish[i] = false` for all $i$; repeatedly find an $i$ with `Finish[i] == false` and $\text{Need}_i \le \text{Work}$, set $\text{Work} \mathrel{+}= \text{Allocation}_i$ and $\text{Finish}[i] = \text{true}$; the state is safe if every `Finish[i]` ends true.

blocks.title: Worked example — Banker's algorithm, one grant and one refusal
blocks.text:
Four processes, three resource types with totals $A = 10$, $B = 3$, $C = 7$.

| Process | Allocation (A,B,C) | Max (A,B,C) | Need = Max − Alloc |
|---|---|---|---|
| $P_0$ | 1, 0, 2 | 4, 1, 3 | 3, 1, 1 |
| $P_1$ | 2, 1, 1 | 3, 2, 4 | 1, 1, 3 |
| $P_2$ | 3, 0, 1 | 6, 1, 2 | 3, 1, 1 |
| $P_3$ | 1, 1, 1 | 2, 2, 3 | 1, 1, 2 |

Allocated totals are $(7, 2, 5)$, so $\text{Available} = (10,3,7) - (7,2,5) = (3, 1, 2)$.

**Is the current state safe?** Work $=(3,1,2)$.
- $P_0$ needs $(3,1,1)$ — fits? $3\le3, 1\le1, 1\le2$: yes, but try $P_3$ first to build the canonical sequence. Taking processes in index order: $P_0$ fits, Work $\to (3,1,2)+(1,0,2)=(4,1,4)$; $P_1$ needs $(1,1,3)$, fits, Work $\to (6,2,5)$; $P_2$ needs $(3,1,1)$, fits, Work $\to (9,2,6)$; $P_3$ needs $(1,1,2)$, fits, Work $\to (10,3,7)$. All four finish, so the state is **safe**, with safe sequence $\langle P_0, P_1, P_2, P_3\rangle$. (Another valid sequence is $\langle P_3, P_0, P_1, P_2\rangle$ — a state is safe if *at least one* sequence exists.)

**Request 1: $P_3$ asks for $(1,0,1)$.**
- $(1,0,1) \le \text{Need}_3 = (1,1,2)$ — legal.
- $(1,0,1) \le \text{Available} = (3,1,2)$ — resources exist.
- Pretend: Available $=(2,1,1)$, $\text{Alloc}_3 = (2,1,2)$, $\text{Need}_3 = (0,1,1)$.
- Safety: Work $=(2,1,1)$. $P_0$ needs $(3,1,1)$ — $3 > 2$, skip. $P_1$ needs $(1,1,3)$ — $3>1$, skip. $P_2$ needs $(3,1,1)$ — skip. $P_3$ needs $(0,1,1) \le (2,1,1)$ — **fits**, Work $\to (2,1,1)+(2,1,2) = (4,2,3)$. Now $P_0$ needs $(3,1,1) \le (4,2,3)$ — fits, Work $\to (5,2,5)$. $P_1$ needs $(1,1,3)\le(5,2,5)$ — fits, Work $\to (7,3,6)$. $P_2$ needs $(3,1,1)\le(7,3,6)$ — fits, Work $\to (10,3,7)$.
- All finish, so the state is safe and the request is **granted**, with sequence $\langle P_3, P_0, P_1, P_2\rangle$.

**Request 2: from the original state, $P_1$ asks for $(1,0,1)$ — the same vector.**
- $(1,0,1) \le \text{Need}_1 = (1,1,3)$ — legal. $(1,0,1) \le (3,1,2)$ — available.
- Pretend: Available $=(2,1,1)$, $\text{Alloc}_1 = (3,1,2)$, $\text{Need}_1 = (0,1,2)$.
- Safety: Work $=(2,1,1)$. $P_0$ needs $(3,1,1)$: $3>2$, no. $P_1$ needs $(0,1,2)$: $2 > 1$ in C, no. $P_2$ needs $(3,1,1)$: no. $P_3$ needs $(1,1,2)$: $2>1$ in C, no.
- No process can finish, so the pretended state is **unsafe** and the request is **denied** — $P_1$ waits even though the resources are physically free.

The same request vector is granted to one process and refused to another. That is the entire point of avoidance: the decision depends on the whole state, not on the request.

blocks.text:
## Detection

If maximum claims are unknown, avoidance is impossible and the system can only detect. For **single-instance** resources, build the **wait-for graph** by collapsing resource nodes out of the resource-allocation graph ($P_i \to P_j$ if $P_i$ waits for something $P_j$ holds) and look for a cycle. Cycle detection on $n$ vertices costs $O(n^2)$.

For **multiple instances**, run an algorithm shaped like the safety algorithm but using the current `Request` matrix instead of `Need` — because a process that is not currently requesting anything is assumed to be able to finish. The cost is $O(m \cdot n^2)$.

How often to run it is a trade-off: on every request that cannot be granted immediately (exact, expensive) or periodically, say once an hour or when CPU utilisation drops below 40% (cheap, but many processes may be involved by then, making it hard to say which one caused it).

**Recovery** is by process termination — abort all deadlocked processes, or abort one at a time until the cycle breaks, choosing by priority, CPU time consumed, resources held, or how much work would be lost — or by **resource preemption**, which needs a victim-selection rule, a rollback strategy (usually total rollback to a safe checkpoint), and a guard against always picking the same victim, which would be **starvation**.

blocks.title: The deadlock-free resource count
blocks.text:
Suppose $n$ processes share $R$ instances of a **single** resource type, and each process may need at most $k$ instances. The worst case is that every process holds $k-1$ instances and waits for one more. If even one instance is left over, some process can complete and release everything. So the system is **guaranteed deadlock-free** exactly when

$$R \ge n(k-1) + 1 \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad R > n(k-1)$$

Rearranged for the other unknowns:

$$n \le \frac{R-1}{k-1}, \qquad k \le \frac{R-1}{n} + 1$$

The general version, when process $i$ has maximum need $m_i \ge 1$:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i < R + n$$

Check the special case: if all $m_i = k$ this reads $nk < R + n$, i.e. $R > n(k-1)$, the same thing.

blocks.title: Worked example — using the deadlock-free formula
blocks.text:
**(a)** Three processes share 4 units of a resource, each needing at most 2. Is deadlock possible?

$n(k-1)+1 = 3(2-1)+1 = 4$. We have $R = 4 \ge 4$, so the system is **deadlock-free**. Sanity check: if all three hold 1 unit each, the 4th unit is free and one process completes.

**(b)** Each of $n$ processes may need up to 3 units and there are 10 units. What is the largest $n$ for which deadlock is impossible?

$n \le \dfrac{R-1}{k-1} = \dfrac{9}{2} = 4.5$, so $n = 4$. With 5 processes, each could hold 2 units, consuming all 10 and leaving nothing — deadlock.

**(c)** Three processes have maximum needs 3, 4 and 5 units of a single resource type. What is the minimum $R$ that guarantees no deadlock?

Use $\sum m_i < R + n$: $3+4+5 = 12 < R + 3$, so $R > 9$, giving $R_{\min} = 10$. Check: with 9 units the processes could hold 2, 3 and 4 respectively, using all 9 with every one still short by exactly 1 — deadlock. With 10, that configuration leaves a spare unit.

blocks.q: A system has 6 instances of a resource type shared by 3 processes. If each process may request a maximum of 3 instances, the system is
opts: deadlock-free only if requests are ordered
blocks.exp: The safe threshold is $R \ge n(k-1)+1 = 3 \times 2 + 1 = 7$. Here $R = 6 < 7$, so deadlock is possible: each process can hold 2 instances, exhausting all 6, with every process still needing one more. 'Possible' is the right word — a lucky interleaving still completes.

blocks.q: Which statement about safe and unsafe states is correct?
opts: Every unsafe state is a deadlocked state
Every safe state may lead to deadlock
Every deadlocked state is unsafe, but not every unsafe state is deadlocked
Safe and unsafe states are unrelated to deadlock
blocks.exp: Safety guarantees a completion order exists, so a safe state can never be deadlocked. Losing that guarantee is not the same as being stuck: from an unsafe state the processes may still all finish if they happen not to claim their full maxima. Hence deadlocked is a strict subset of unsafe.

tricks.title: $R \ge n(k-1)+1$ answers a whole question family
tricks.body: Whichever of $R$, $n$ or $k$ is missing, rearrange this one inequality. Remember it as 'everybody holds one short of their maximum, plus one spare unit'.

tricks.title: Run the safety algorithm in index order
tricks.body: You do not need the cleverest sequence, only *some* sequence. Scan $P_0, P_1, \ldots$ repeatedly, taking the first process that fits, and restart the scan after each success. If a full scan finds nobody, the state is unsafe — stop there.

tricks.title: Compute Need first, always
tricks.body: Every Banker's question starts by filling in $\text{Need} = \text{Max} - \text{Allocation}$ and $\text{Available} = \text{Total} - \sum \text{Allocation}$. Half the marks are lost by people who compare Max against Available instead of Need.

tricks.title: One resource type makes it a counting problem
tricks.body: With a single resource type you never need the matrix version. Total held plus available is fixed; a state is safe iff some process's remaining need is no more than what is free.

traps.title: Unsafe is not deadlocked
traps.body: This is the single most exploited confusion in the topic. Banker's algorithm refuses requests that lead to unsafe states precisely because it cannot tell which unsafe states will become deadlocks, not because they already are deadlocks.

traps.title: A cycle is not always a deadlock
traps.body: Only with one instance per resource type does a cycle guarantee deadlock. With multiple instances a cycle is necessary but not sufficient — a process outside the cycle can release an instance and free everyone.

traps.title: Avoidance needs advance knowledge, detection does not
traps.body: The Banker's algorithm cannot run without declared maximum claims. If a question states that maximum needs are unknown, avoidance is off the table and only detection or prevention applies.
