topics.summary: Contiguous allocation and fragmentation, paging, segmentation, the TLB and effective access time.

blocks.text:
## Binding, and why addresses must be translated

A program refers to addresses symbolically; at some point each symbol must become a physical location. **Binding** can happen at compile time (absolute code, must load at a fixed place), at load time (relocatable code, fixed once loaded) or at **execution time**, which is what every modern system does because it allows a process to be moved while running. Execution-time binding needs hardware: the **memory management unit (MMU)**.

The address a program generates is a **logical (virtual) address**; the address the memory sees is a **physical address**. In the simplest MMU the translation is one addition — a relocation register holding the base is added to every logical address, and a limit register catches out-of-range references. The set of logical addresses a process can generate is its **logical address space**; the user program never sees a physical address at all.

## Contiguous allocation and fragmentation

Give each process one contiguous block. Memory then becomes a mixture of allocated partitions and **holes**, and the allocator must choose a hole for each arriving process.

| Strategy | Rule | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **First fit** | first hole large enough | fastest; good in practice |
| **Best fit** | smallest hole large enough | best space utilisation; must search the whole list; leaves slivers |
| **Worst fit** | largest hole | intended to leave usable remainders; in practice the worst of the three |
| Next fit | first fit, resuming from the last position | spreads allocation around |

Two kinds of waste arise:

- **External fragmentation** — total free memory is enough, but it is split into pieces none of which is big enough. This is the disease of contiguous allocation and segmentation. The cure is **compaction** (shuffle everything to one end, possible only with execution-time binding) or abandoning contiguity altogether, which is what paging does. The **50-percent rule** says that with first fit, if $N$ blocks are allocated, about $0.5N$ blocks are lost to fragmentation, so roughly one third of memory can be unusable.
- **Internal fragmentation** — memory handed out inside a fixed-size unit but not used, for example the unused tail of the last page. This is the disease of paging and fixed partitioning. On average a process wastes half a page, so with page size $p$ the expected internal fragmentation per process is $p/2$.

blocks.title: Worked example — first fit, best fit and worst fit
blocks.text:
Free holes in order of address: **150 KB, 480 KB, 220 KB, 330 KB, 620 KB**. Processes arrive needing **210 KB, 420 KB, 110 KB, 430 KB**, in that order.

**First fit.**
- 210 → first hole $\ge 210$ is 480; leaves 270. Holes: 150, 270, 220, 330, 620.
- 420 → first hole $\ge 420$ is 620; leaves 200. Holes: 150, 270, 220, 330, 200.
- 110 → first hole $\ge 110$ is 150; leaves 40. Holes: 40, 270, 220, 330, 200.
- 430 → no hole is large enough. **Fails**, although $40+270+220+330+200 = 1060$ KB is free.

**Best fit.**
- 210 → smallest hole $\ge 210$ is 220; leaves 10. Holes: 150, 480, 10, 330, 620.
- 420 → smallest $\ge 420$ is 480; leaves 60. Holes: 150, 60, 10, 330, 620.
- 110 → smallest $\ge 110$ is 150; leaves 40. Holes: 40, 60, 10, 330, 620.
- 430 → smallest $\ge 430$ is 620; leaves 190. **All four are placed.**

**Worst fit.**
- 210 → largest hole 620; leaves 410. Holes: 150, 480, 220, 330, 410.
- 420 → largest $\ge 420$ is 480; leaves 60. Holes: 150, 60, 220, 330, 410.
- 110 → largest hole 410; leaves 300. Holes: 150, 60, 220, 330, 300.
- 430 → largest hole is 330, too small. **Fails.**

So best fit succeeds here and the other two do not. That is not a general law — the usual finding is that first fit and best fit both beat worst fit, with first fit faster — but it shows exactly how the strategies diverge.

## Paging

Paging removes the requirement that a process occupy contiguous physical memory. Physical memory is divided into fixed-size **frames**, the logical address space into **pages** of the same size, and a **page table** maps page numbers to frame numbers.

If the page size is $2^{n}$ bytes and the logical address is $m$ bits wide, then the low $n$ bits are the **offset** and the high $m-n$ bits are the **page number**:

$$\underbrace{p}_{m-n\text{ bits}} \; \underbrace{d}_{n\text{ bits}} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{physical address} = f \times 2^{n} + d$$

The offset is never translated — it is copied through unchanged. Page size is always a power of two exactly so that the split is a bit-slice rather than a division.

Paging produces **no external fragmentation** (any free frame fits any page) but does produce internal fragmentation in the last page of each process. A page-table entry typically holds the frame number plus a valid/invalid bit, protection bits, a modify (dirty) bit and a reference bit.

The cost is that every memory reference now needs *two* physical accesses: one to read the page-table entry, one to read the datum. For a $k$-level page table it becomes $k+1$.

blocks.title: Page-table size
blocks.text:
Number of entries $= \dfrac{\text{logical address space}}{\text{page size}}$, and page-table size $=$ entries $\times$ entry size.

A 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages has $2^{32}/2^{12} = 2^{20}$ entries; at 4 bytes each that is **4 MB of page table per process** — far too large to keep contiguously in memory, which is why hierarchical, hashed and inverted page tables exist.

An **inverted page table** has one entry per *physical frame* rather than per virtual page, so its size depends on physical memory, not on the number of processes. It saves enormous space but makes lookup a search (normally hashed) and makes shared memory awkward.

## The TLB and effective access time

The **translation lookaside buffer** is a small fully associative cache of recent page-table entries, searched in parallel with a tiny access time $t$. On a hit, the frame number is available immediately and only the data access costs main memory time $m$. On a miss, the page table must be read from memory first.

$$\text{EAT} = h\,(t + m) + (1-h)\,(t + 2m)$$

which simplifies to

$$\text{EAT} = t + m + (1-h)\,m = t + (2-h)\,m$$

with $h$ the hit ratio. If the question says the TLB lookup time is negligible or is overlapped, drop $t$ and use $\text{EAT} = h\,m + (1-h)\,2m$. Always state the assumption you used — examiners accept both conventions but the numbers differ.

In a multilevel scheme with $k$ levels, a TLB miss costs $k$ memory accesses for the tables plus one for the data, so

$$\text{EAT} = h\,(t+m) + (1-h)\,(t + (k+1)m)$$

The TLB must be handled on a context switch: either **flush** it, which costs a burst of misses afterwards, or tag each entry with an **address-space identifier (ASID)** so entries from different processes can coexist.

blocks.title: Worked example — effective access time
blocks.text:
Main memory access time is 100 ns, TLB access time is 20 ns, and the TLB hit ratio is 80%. The page table is single-level and lives in main memory.

- **Hit** (probability 0.8): search the TLB (20 ns) and then read the data (100 ns) $= 120$ ns.
- **Miss** (probability 0.2): search the TLB (20 ns), read the page-table entry from memory (100 ns), then read the data (100 ns) $= 220$ ns.

$$\text{EAT} = 0.8 \times 120 + 0.2 \times 220 = 96 + 44 = \mathbf{140\ \text{ns}}$$

Without any TLB at all the cost would be a flat 200 ns, so the 80% hit ratio buys a 30% reduction.

**What hit ratio is needed for an EAT of 130 ns?** Using $\text{EAT} = t + (2-h)m$: $130 = 20 + (2-h)\times 100$, so $(2-h) = 1.1$ and $h = 0.9$.

**Same machine, two-level page table, 80% hit ratio.** A miss now costs $20 + 100 + 100 + 100 = 320$ ns, so $\text{EAT} = 0.8 \times 120 + 0.2 \times 320 = 96 + 64 = 160$ ns. Each extra level of paging costs $(1-h)\times m = 20$ ns here.

## Segmentation, and segmentation with paging

Paging is invisible to the programmer and splits memory at arbitrary boundaries. **Segmentation** instead divides the address space the way the programmer thinks of it: a code segment, a stack segment, a symbol-table segment, one segment per array. A logical address is a pair $\langle s, d \rangle$ and the **segment table** holds, for each segment, a **base** and a **limit**. Translation is: if $d \ge \text{limit}$ raise a trap, else physical address $=$ base $+\; d$.

| | Paging | Segmentation |
|---|---|---|
| Block size | fixed | variable |
| Chosen by | hardware/OS | programmer/compiler |
| Address | one number, split by hardware | explicit pair $\langle s,d\rangle$ |
| External fragmentation | none | yes |
| Internal fragmentation | yes (last page) | none |
| Protection granularity | per page, arbitrary boundaries | per logical object — natural |
| Table entry | frame number | base and limit |

**Segmentation with paging** takes both: the address space is segmented, and each segment is then paged, so the segment table points to a page table rather than to memory. This removes external fragmentation while keeping logical protection, at the cost of another level of lookup. The Intel 386 architecture used exactly this scheme.

blocks.q: A machine has 16-bit logical addresses and a page size of 1 KB. How many bits are used for the page number?
blocks.exp: A 1 KB page is $2^{10}$ bytes, so the offset uses 10 bits. The remaining $16 - 10 = 6$ bits are the page number, giving $2^{6} = 64$ pages per process. The offset width is always $\log_2(\text{page size})$.

blocks.q: Memory access takes 80 ns, TLB access takes 10 ns, and the hit ratio is 90%. The effective access time is
blocks.exp: Hits cost $10 + 80 = 90$ ns and misses cost $10 + 80 + 80 = 170$ ns, so $\text{EAT} = 0.9(90) + 0.1(170) = 81 + 17 = 98$ ns. Equivalently $t + (2-h)m = 10 + 1.1 \times 80 = 98$.

tricks.title: EAT in one step
tricks.body: When the page table is single-level and in memory, $\text{EAT} = t + (2-h)m$. With $k$ levels it becomes $\text{EAT} = t + \big(1 + (1-h)k\big)m$. Memorise the compact form and you avoid writing two products.

tricks.title: Offset bits equal $\log_2$(page size) — nothing else changes
tricks.body: Whatever the question, split the address at the page size first. The offset is identical in the logical and physical address, so any option showing a different offset is wrong immediately.

tricks.title: Fragmentation by allocation unit
tricks.body: Fixed-size units (paging, fixed partitions) cause internal fragmentation. Variable-size units (segmentation, dynamic partitions) cause external fragmentation. Paging plus segmentation gets internal only. Answering these needs no calculation.

tricks.title: Page-table size is a two-step division
tricks.body: Entries $=$ address space $\div$ page size; size $=$ entries $\times$ entry width. Watch for questions that give physical memory instead — that determines the *frame number width*, not the number of entries.

traps.title: Number of pages versus number of frames
traps.body: Pages are counted from the *logical* address space, frames from *physical* memory. The two are usually different, and the frame number field can be narrower or wider than the page number field. A 32-bit logical space with 1 GB of physical RAM and 4 KB pages has $2^{20}$ pages and $2^{18}$ frames.

traps.title: Compaction cannot fix internal fragmentation
traps.body: Compaction moves partitions together to merge free holes, so it addresses external fragmentation only. Nothing recovers the unused tail of a page except a smaller page size, which increases the page table instead.

traps.title: Paging does not by itself give virtual memory
traps.body: Pure paging still requires every page of a process to be resident. Virtual memory needs *demand* paging with the valid/invalid bit and a page-fault handler, which is the next topic.

topics.title: Virtual Memory and Page Replacement
topics.summary: Demand paging, page-fault cost, every replacement algorithm, Belady's anomaly, thrashing and the working set.

blocks.text:
## Demand paging

Virtual memory lets a process run when only part of it is in memory. Each page-table entry carries a **valid/invalid bit**: valid means the page is resident and the frame number is meaningful, invalid means either the page is illegal or it is on the backing store. A reference to an invalid-but-legal page raises a **page fault**, a trap the OS handles.

Handling a page fault:

1. The trap transfers control to the OS, which saves the process state.
2. Check an internal table: is this reference legal? If not, terminate the process.
3. Find a free frame. If none is free, run the **page-replacement algorithm** to choose a victim; if the victim's **dirty bit** is set, write it back to disk first.
4. Schedule a disk read to bring the wanted page into the frame.
5. When the I/O completes, update the page table (set valid, set the frame number) and the internal tables.
6. Restart the instruction that faulted, from the beginning.

Step 6 is why the hardware must be able to restart any instruction. A block-move instruction that has already copied half its bytes, or an auto-increment addressing mode that has already bumped a register, has to be undone or made restartable — this is a genuine architectural constraint, not a detail.

The benefits: more processes fit in memory, a process may be larger than physical memory, and less I/O is needed at load time because only the pages actually touched are read. **Copy-on-write** applies the same idea to `fork`: parent and child share every page read-only, and only a page that is written gets duplicated.

blocks.title: Effective access time with page faults
blocks.text:
With memory access time $m$, page-fault rate $p$ and fault service time $F$:

$$\text{EAT} = (1-p)\,m + p\,F$$

The fault service time includes trap handling, possibly writing back a dirty page, the disk read, and restart — and it is measured in **milliseconds** while $m$ is in **nanoseconds**, a ratio of about $10^5$. That is why $p$ must be astonishingly small.

If a victim is dirty with probability $q$, the service time becomes $F_{\text{clean}}$ plus $q$ times a write-back, so

$$\text{EAT} = (1-p)\,m + p\big[(1-q)F + q(F + W)\big]$$

blocks.title: Worked example — how small must the fault rate be?
blocks.text:
Memory access time is 200 ns and servicing a page fault takes 8 ms.

**(a) Fault rate 0.001 (one fault per 1000 accesses).**

$8\ \text{ms} = 8{,}000{,}000$ ns, so

$$\text{EAT} = (1 - 0.001)(200) + (0.001)(8{,}000{,}000) = 199.8 + 8000 = 8199.8\ \text{ns} \approx 8.2\ \mu\text{s}$$

That is a **slowdown of about 41 times** from a fault rate of one in a thousand.

**(b) What fault rate keeps the degradation under 10%?**

We need $\text{EAT} \le 220$ ns.

$$200(1-p) + 8{,}000{,}000\,p \le 220 \;\Longrightarrow\; 7{,}999{,}800\,p \le 20 \;\Longrightarrow\; p \le 2.5 \times 10^{-6}$$

So fewer than one fault in 400,000 memory accesses. This single calculation is the justification for everything else in the topic: locality of reference, careful replacement policies, and the working-set model all exist to keep $p$ at that level.

## The replacement algorithms

Given a **reference string** (the sequence of page numbers touched) and a number of frames, each algorithm picks a victim differently.

- **FIFO** — evict the page that has been in memory longest. Implemented with a queue; cheap. It can evict a heavily used page simply because it arrived early, and it suffers **Belady's anomaly**.
- **Optimal (OPT, MIN, Belady's algorithm)** — evict the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future. It gives the provably minimum number of faults, but it needs the future, so it exists only as a benchmark.
- **LRU** — evict the page unused for the longest time. It is OPT looking backwards, and it works because of locality. Exact implementations need either a counter written into the page-table entry on every reference or a doubly linked stack updated on every reference — both far too expensive without hardware help.
- **Second chance (clock)** — FIFO plus the **reference bit**. Scan the circular list; if the candidate's reference bit is 0 evict it, if it is 1 clear the bit and move on, giving that page another lap. A page referenced often is never evicted; if every bit is set, the algorithm degenerates to FIFO.
- **Enhanced second chance** — use the (reference, modify) pair and prefer to evict $(0,0)$, then $(0,1)$, then $(1,0)$, then $(1,1)$, so clean pages go first and a disk write is avoided.
- **LFU** — evict the page with the smallest reference count. It behaves badly when a page was heavily used early and is never needed again; counts must be aged.
- **MFU** — evict the most-used page, on the argument that a page with a small count has just arrived and will be needed. Rarely useful; it appears in questions as a name to recognise.

blocks.title: Worked example — the same string under FIFO, LRU and OPT
blocks.text:
Reference string: **1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5**

**FIFO with 3 frames.**

| Ref | Frames after | Fault? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | F |
| 2 | 1 2 | F |
| 3 | 1 2 3 | F |
| 4 | 2 3 4 | F (evict 1) |
| 1 | 3 4 1 | F (evict 2) |
| 2 | 4 1 2 | F (evict 3) |
| 5 | 1 2 5 | F (evict 4) |
| 1 | 1 2 5 | hit |
| 2 | 1 2 5 | hit |
| 3 | 2 5 3 | F (evict 1) |
| 4 | 5 3 4 | F (evict 2) |
| 5 | 5 3 4 | hit |

**9 faults.**

**FIFO with 4 frames.** Loading 1,2,3,4 costs 4 faults; 1 and 2 then hit; 5 evicts 1; 1 evicts 2; 2 evicts 3; 3 evicts 4; 4 evicts 5; 5 evicts 1. That is $4 + 6 = $ **10 faults** — *more* faults with *more* frames. This is **Belady's anomaly**.

**LRU with 3 frames.** 1,2,3 fault; 4 evicts 1; 1 evicts 2; 2 evicts 3; 5 evicts 4; 1 and 2 hit; 3 evicts 5; 4 evicts 1; 5 evicts 2. **10 faults.** With 4 frames LRU gives **8 faults** — never worse, because LRU is a stack algorithm.

**OPT with 3 frames.** 1,2,3 fault. At 4, the next uses are 1 at position 5, 2 at position 6, 3 at position 10, so evict 3. Then 1 and 2 hit. At 5, the resident pages 1, 2, 4 are next used at positions 8, 9 and 11, so evict 4. Then 1 and 2 hit again. At 3, pages 1 and 2 are never used again — evict 1. At 4, evict 2 for the same reason. Then 5 hits. **7 faults**, the minimum possible.

| Algorithm | 3 frames | 4 frames |
|---|---|---|
| OPT | 7 | 6 |
| LRU | 10 | 8 |
| FIFO | 9 | **10** |

Notice that FIFO beats LRU at 3 frames. LRU is usually better but is not guaranteed to be — only OPT is guaranteed optimal.

blocks.title: Belady's anomaly and stack algorithms
blocks.text:
An algorithm is a **stack algorithm** if, for every reference string, the set of pages resident with $n$ frames is always a **subset** of the set resident with $n+1$ frames. Stack algorithms cannot exhibit Belady's anomaly.

- **LRU and OPT are stack algorithms** — immune to the anomaly.
- **FIFO is not**, and neither is second chance/clock, which is FIFO-based.

So the answer to 'which of the following suffers from Belady's anomaly' is FIFO (and clock variants), never LRU and never OPT.

blocks.title: Try it — page replacement
blocks.note: Type a reference string, set the frame count, and step through FIFO, LRU, OPT and clock; try 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 at 3 and 4 frames to see Belady's anomaly.

blocks.text:
## Frame allocation and thrashing

Every process needs a **minimum number of frames** set by the instruction set: enough to hold the instruction and all the operands it may reference at once, otherwise an instruction could fault forever without completing.

Allocation policies: **equal allocation** ($m/n$ frames each), **proportional allocation** (frames in proportion to process size, $a_i = s_i/S \times m$), or priority-weighted variants. Replacement may be **global** (a process may steal a frame from another process — better throughput, but a process's fault rate now depends on other processes' behaviour) or **local** (a process replaces only among its own frames — predictable, but a process cannot use idle frames elsewhere).

**Thrashing** is the state where processes spend more time paging than executing. It begins when a process does not have enough frames to hold its current locality: it faults, which takes a frame from someone else, who then faults, and so on. The signature is high paging I/O with collapsing CPU utilisation — and the disastrous feedback loop is that a scheduler measuring low CPU utilisation responds by admitting *more* processes, which makes it worse.

Two controls:

- **Working-set model.** The working set $WSS_i$ is the set of pages referenced in the last $\Delta$ references. If $D = \sum WSS_i$ exceeds the number of frames $m$, thrashing is occurring and the OS should suspend a process. Choosing $\Delta$ matters: too small and it misses the locality, too large and it spans several localities.
- **Page-fault frequency (PFF).** Set an upper and a lower bound on each process's fault rate. Above the upper bound, give it another frame; below the lower bound, take one away. This measures the symptom directly rather than estimating the working set.

blocks.q: Which of the following page-replacement algorithms can suffer from Belady's anomaly?
blocks.exp: LRU and OPT are stack algorithms: the pages resident with $n$ frames are always a subset of those resident with $n+1$, so adding a frame can never add a fault. FIFO has no such property — its victim choice ignores usage entirely — and the string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4.

blocks.q: Memory access takes 100 ns and a page fault takes 10 ms to service. For the effective access time to be at most 200 ns, the page-fault rate must be at most approximately
blocks.exp: $\text{EAT} = (1-p)(100) + p(10^{7})\ \text{ns} \le 200$ gives $p(10^{7} - 100) \le 100$, so $p \le 100/9{,}999{,}900 \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$. Doubling the access time tolerates only one fault per hundred thousand references — the disk is five orders of magnitude slower than memory.

tricks.title: Count faults, not hits, and remember cold misses
tricks.body: Every distinct page costs one compulsory fault the first time it appears. So the fault count is never below the number of distinct pages in the string, and if the frame count is at least the number of distinct pages the answer is exactly that number, whatever the algorithm.

tricks.title: OPT: look forward, evict the one you need latest
tricks.body: At each fault, write next to each resident page the position of its next occurrence, using $\infty$ if it never reappears. Evict the largest. Pages that never reappear go first and make the rest quick.

tricks.title: LRU backwards equals OPT forwards
tricks.body: To run LRU quickly, read the reference string *leftwards* from the current point and evict the resident page you meet last. That is mechanically identical to the OPT rule with the string reversed, so one habit serves both algorithms.

tricks.title: Stack property settles all anomaly questions
tricks.body: If the algorithm's victim depends only on the order of past references (LRU, OPT, LFU by count), it is a stack algorithm and shows no anomaly. If it depends on arrival order into memory (FIFO, clock), it can.

traps.title: LRU is not always better than FIFO
traps.body: On the string above, FIFO takes 9 faults with 3 frames and LRU takes 10. LRU is better *on average* on real workloads, not on every string. Options asserting that LRU always gives fewer faults than FIFO are false.

traps.title: A page fault is not a memory-protection error
traps.body: A fault on a legal but non-resident page is serviced transparently and the instruction restarts. A reference outside the address space is an invalid-reference trap that kills the process. Both set the same valid bit to 0, which is why the OS needs a separate internal table.

traps.title: Thrashing is not solved by adding processes
traps.body: The scheduler's instinct — low CPU utilisation, admit more work — is exactly wrong. The cure is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming, or give the suffering process more frames.

traps.title: Second chance is not LRU
traps.body: The clock algorithm approximates LRU with a single reference bit and can evict a page used quite recently. Questions that call clock 'an implementation of LRU' overstate it; the correct word is approximation.

topics.title: Storage Management, Disk Scheduling and RAID
topics.summary: Disk geometry and access time, all six scheduling algorithms compared on one request queue, and the RAID levels.

blocks.text:
## Disk geometry and the cost of a read

A magnetic disk is a stack of platters; each surface is divided into concentric **tracks**, each track into **sectors**. The set of tracks at the same radius across all surfaces is a **cylinder** — the important unit, because all the heads move together on one arm, so the whole cylinder is reachable without another seek.

The time to service a request has three parts:

$$\text{Access time} = \text{seek time} + \text{rotational latency} + \text{transfer time}$$

- **Seek time** — move the arm to the right cylinder. Milliseconds, and by far the largest and most variable term. It is the only part a scheduler can influence, which is why every disk-scheduling algorithm is about minimising head movement.
- **Rotational latency** — wait for the sector to arrive under the head. On average **half a revolution**, so for a disk at $r$ RPM the average latency is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{60}{r}$ seconds.
- **Transfer time** — read the bytes as they pass. Proportional to the amount of data divided by the transfer rate.

Solid-state drives have no arm and no rotation, so seek and latency vanish, scheduling matters far less, and the dominant concerns become write amplification and wear levelling.

blocks.title: Worked example — disk access time
blocks.text:
A disk rotates at 7200 RPM, has an average seek time of 5 ms, and transfers at 100 MB/s. How long does an average 4 KB read take?

- One revolution takes $\dfrac{60}{7200} = 8.33$ ms, so the **average rotational latency** is $8.33/2 = 4.17$ ms.
- **Transfer**: $\dfrac{4096\ \text{bytes}}{100 \times 10^{6}\ \text{bytes/s}} = 40.96\ \mu\text{s} \approx 0.04$ ms.
- **Total** $= 5 + 4.17 + 0.04 = \mathbf{9.21\ \text{ms}}$.

The transfer is 0.4% of the cost and the mechanical delays are 99.6%. That is the entire economic argument for large block sizes, for read-ahead, and for scheduling.

**A second version.** If the disk has 500 sectors per track of 512 bytes, one track holds 256 KB and passes under the head in 8.33 ms, giving an implied transfer rate of $256/8.33 \approx 30.7$ MB/s. Reading a whole track costs $5 + 4.17 + 8.33 = 17.5$ ms — barely twice the cost of one sector for 64 times the data.

## The scheduling algorithms

- **FCFS** — serve in arrival order. Fair, never starves, and usually terrible, because consecutive requests can be at opposite ends.
- **SSTF** — serve the request closest to the current head position. Much better average movement, but it is essentially shortest-job-first for the disk arm, so it can **starve** requests at the edges while a cluster near the middle keeps being served.
- **SCAN (elevator)** — the head sweeps from one end of the disk to the other, servicing everything on the way, then reverses. It **goes all the way to cylinder 0 and to the last cylinder** even if no request is waiting there. No starvation; a request just behind the head must wait for a full sweep out and back.
- **C-SCAN** — sweep in one direction only. On reaching the end, jump straight back to the start without servicing anything and begin again. This makes the wait time **uniform** for all cylinders, whereas plain SCAN favours the middle, where the head passes twice as often.
- **LOOK** — SCAN, but reverse at the **last request** in the current direction rather than at the physical end of the disk.
- **C-LOOK** — C-SCAN with the same improvement: go as far as the furthest request, then jump back to the **lowest** pending request.

In practice LOOK and C-LOOK are what real drivers implement; SCAN and C-SCAN are the textbook idealisations.

blocks.title: Worked example — one request queue, six algorithms
blocks.text:
A disk has cylinders **0 to 199**. The head is at **50** and was last moving **towards higher** cylinder numbers. The pending queue, in arrival order, is

**82, 170, 43, 140, 24, 16, 190**

**FCFS.** $|50-82| + |82-170| + |170-43| + |43-140| + |140-24| + |24-16| + |16-190|$
$= 32 + 88 + 127 + 97 + 116 + 8 + 174 = \mathbf{642}$ cylinders.

**SSTF.** From 50 the nearest is 43 (7). From 43 the nearest is 24 (19). Then 16 (8). Then the nearest remaining is 82 (66). Then 140 (58), 170 (30), 190 (20).
Order: 43, 24, 16, 82, 140, 170, 190. Total $= 7+19+8+66+58+30+20 = \mathbf{208}$.

**SCAN** (moving up). Service 82, 140, 170, 190, continue to **199**, reverse, then 43, 24, 16.
Total $= (199-50) + (199-16) = 149 + 183 = \mathbf{332}$.

**C-SCAN** (moving up). Service 82, 140, 170, 190, go to 199, jump to 0, then service 16, 24, 43.
Total $= 149 + 199 + 43 = \mathbf{391}$ (counting the return sweep).

**LOOK** (moving up). Service 82, 140, 170, 190 — stop there, no request above — reverse and service 43, 24, 16.
Total $= (190-50) + (190-16) = 140 + 174 = \mathbf{314}$.

**C-LOOK** (moving up). Service 82, 140, 170, 190, jump back to the lowest request 16, then 24, 43.
Total $= 140 + 174 + 27 = \mathbf{341}$.

| Algorithm | Head movement |
|---|---|
| FCFS | 642 |
| **SSTF** | **208** |
| SCAN | 332 |
| C-SCAN | 391 |
| LOOK | 314 |
| C-LOOK | 341 |

SSTF wins on this queue, as it usually does on total distance — but it is the one algorithm here that can starve a request indefinitely. Note also that the circular variants cost *more* total movement than their non-circular partners; what they buy is fairness, not distance.

blocks.title: Try it — disk scheduling
blocks.note: Set the head position, direction and request queue, and compare the seek sequences and totals for FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK and C-LOOK.

blocks.title: The two things that change the answer
blocks.text:
1. **Direction.** SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK and C-LOOK all need to know whether the head is currently moving up or down. Reversing the assumed direction changes the total. If a question does not state it, say which you assumed.
2. **Whether the return jump counts.** For C-SCAN and C-LOOK, most textbooks and most exam keys **include** the jump back in the total head movement. Some sources exclude it. Include it unless told otherwise, and note that the *relative ordering* of the algorithms rarely changes either way.

## RAID

RAID combines several physical disks into one logical device for **performance** (by striping) and **reliability** (by redundancy).

| Level | Technique | Usable capacity of $n$ disks | Failures tolerated |
|---|---|---|---|
| RAID 0 | block striping, no redundancy | $n$ | **0** |
| RAID 1 | mirroring | $n/2$ | 1 per mirrored pair |
| RAID 2 | bit striping with Hamming ECC | $\approx n - \log n$ | 1 (obsolete) |
| RAID 3 | byte striping, dedicated parity disk | $n-1$ | 1 |
| RAID 4 | block striping, dedicated parity disk | $n-1$ | 1 |
| RAID 5 | block striping, **distributed** parity | $n-1$ | 1 |
| RAID 6 | block striping, dual distributed parity (P+Q) | $n-2$ | **2** |
| RAID 10 (1+0) | mirror pairs, then stripe | $n/2$ | 1 per pair, often more |
| RAID 01 (0+1) | stripe sets, then mirror | $n/2$ | 1 (a second failure in the other stripe kills it) |

Parity is computed by XOR across the stripe: $P = D_0 \oplus D_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus D_{n-2}$. Any single missing block is recovered by XOR-ing everything that survives, which is why one parity disk protects against exactly one failure.

**RAID 4 versus RAID 5.** With a dedicated parity disk, every write updates parity, so the parity disk becomes a bottleneck and wears out first. RAID 5 rotates the parity block across all disks, spreading that load — which is why RAID 5 replaced RAID 4 in practice.

**The small-write penalty.** Updating one block in RAID 4 or 5 takes **four** I/O operations: read the old data, read the old parity, write the new data, write the new parity (new parity $=$ old parity $\oplus$ old data $\oplus$ new data). RAID 6 costs six. RAID 1 costs two writes and RAID 0 costs one.

**RAID is not a backup.** It protects against disk failure, not against deletion, corruption, ransomware or fire.

## Other storage management topics

**Disk formatting.** *Low-level (physical)* formatting writes the sector headers, data areas and ECC trailers. *Logical* formatting writes the file system's data structures. The **boot block** holds the bootstrap loader; on a system disk this is the partition marked bootable.

**Bad-block handling.** Simple controllers keep a list and the OS avoids them; modern drives do **sector sparing** (remap a bad sector to a spare) or **sector slipping** (shift every sector down by one to keep the sequence contiguous, preserving sequential-access performance).

**Swap space.** It can live in the file system as a large file — flexible but slow, because it goes through the file-system layer — or in a raw partition with its own allocator, which is faster and the usual choice. Linux allows both.

**Storage attachment.** *Host-attached* (SATA, SAS, USB), *network-attached storage* (NAS — a file-level protocol such as NFS or CIFS over the LAN), and *storage-area network* (SAN — block-level access over a dedicated fabric such as Fibre Channel). NAS serves files; SAN serves blocks. That one-line distinction is the exam's whole interest in the subject.

blocks.q: A disk rotates at 6000 RPM. The average rotational latency is
blocks.exp: One revolution takes $60/6000 = 0.01$ s $= 10$ ms. The requested sector is on average half a revolution away, so the average latency is $10/2 = 5$ ms. Be careful not to report the full rotation time, which is the distractor at 10 ms.

blocks.q: Which pair of statements correctly distinguishes SCAN from LOOK?
opts: SCAN reverses at the last request; LOOK goes to the end of the disk
SCAN goes to the end of the disk; LOOK reverses at the last request
Both reverse at the last request, but LOOK is circular
SCAN never reverses; LOOK reverses at the end
blocks.exp: SCAN is the naive elevator: it always travels to cylinder 0 and to the highest cylinder, even when nothing is pending there. LOOK 'looks ahead', finds no further request and turns around early, so its total head movement is never greater than SCAN's.

tricks.title: Compute head movement as endpoints, not steps
tricks.body: For SCAN, LOOK and their circular forms you do not need to add the gaps one by one. SCAN up $= (\text{top} - \text{start}) + (\text{top} - \text{lowest request})$. LOOK up $= (\text{highest request} - \text{start}) + (\text{highest request} - \text{lowest request})$. C-LOOK up $= (\text{highest} - \text{start}) + (\text{highest} - \text{lowest}) + (\text{second lowest} - \text{lowest})$, and similarly downwards.

tricks.title: LOOK $\le$ SCAN and C-LOOK $\le$ C-SCAN, always
tricks.body: Each pair differs only by the extra distance to the physical ends, so the 'LOOK' version can never move further. If your computed numbers break that, you have made a slip.

tricks.title: RAID capacity in one glance
tricks.body: Striping keeps everything ($n$), mirroring halves it ($n/2$), single parity costs one disk ($n-1$), dual parity costs two ($n-2$). Failures tolerated: 0, 1, 1, 2 respectively.

tricks.title: Average latency is always half a rotation
tricks.body: $\text{avg latency} = 30/\text{RPM}$ seconds $= 30000/\text{RPM}$ milliseconds. For 5400, 7200, 10000 and 15000 RPM that is 5.56, 4.17, 3.0 and 2.0 ms — worth remembering as sanity checks.

traps.title: SCAN versus C-SCAN fairness
traps.body: C-SCAN moves *more* total distance than SCAN but gives more *uniform* waiting times, because in plain SCAN the middle cylinders are passed twice per sweep and the ends once. A question asking which minimises variance of waiting time wants C-SCAN; one asking which minimises total movement does not.

traps.title: RAID 0 has no redundancy at all
traps.body: Despite the name, RAID 0 makes reliability strictly *worse*: with $n$ disks the array fails if any one fails, so the mean time to failure is roughly $1/n$ of a single disk's. It is chosen purely for speed and capacity.

traps.title: RAID 01 is not RAID 10
traps.body: RAID 10 mirrors first and then stripes, so after one failure only that mirror pair is degraded. RAID 01 stripes first and then mirrors, so one failure takes out an entire stripe set and a second failure anywhere in the surviving set destroys the array. RAID 10 is the more robust and is what people usually mean.

topics.title: File and Input/Output Systems
topics.summary: File allocation methods and their access costs, directory and free-space structures, and how I/O actually reaches the device.

blocks.text:
## Files, attributes and access methods

A **file** is the OS's abstraction of stored information: a named, persistent sequence of bytes or records. Its **attributes** — name, unique identifier, type, location, size, protection, timestamps — live in the directory entry, not in the file's data.

**Access methods:**

- **Sequential** — read or write the next record; supports `read_next`, `write_next`, `reset` and sometimes skipping forward. This is the model of tapes and of ordinary editor and compiler I/O.
- **Direct (relative)** — the file is a numbered sequence of fixed-length blocks and any block may be read immediately. Databases need this.
- **Indexed** — an index file maps a key to a block number; you search the index, then go to the block. Large files need a multi-level index, which is where B-trees come in.

**Directory structures** progress in obvious steps: single-level (one namespace for everyone, name collisions), two-level (one directory per user), tree (the familiar one, with absolute and relative paths), **acyclic graph** (shared subdirectories via links, needs reference counting for deletion), and **general graph** (cycles are allowed, so reference counting is not enough and garbage collection is required). A **hard link** is a second directory entry pointing at the same inode and keeps the file alive until the last link is removed; a **soft (symbolic) link** is a small file containing a path and dangles if the target is deleted.

## File allocation methods

This is where the marks are. Each method answers one question — which disk blocks hold this file, and how do we find them?

**Contiguous allocation.** The file occupies consecutive blocks; the directory stores a start block and a length. *Advantages:* both sequential and direct access are ideal, and seek time is minimal because the blocks are adjacent — the address of block $i$ is simply $\text{start} + i$, so **one disk access** reaches any block. *Disadvantages:* external fragmentation, and the file cannot grow unless the space after it happens to be free. Used for CD-ROMs and for extent-based file systems, which soften the problem by allocating several contiguous *extents* per file.

**Linked allocation.** Each block contains a pointer to the next; the directory stores the first and last block. *Advantages:* no external fragmentation, files grow freely. *Disadvantages:* direct access is impossible — reaching block $i$ costs $i+1$ reads following the chain; a single corrupted pointer loses the rest of the file; and part of every block is consumed by the pointer, so the usable block size is not a power of two.

**FAT (file allocation table).** Linked allocation with the pointers pulled out into a table at the front of the volume, one entry per disk block. Following the chain then costs table lookups rather than block reads, and if the FAT is cached, direct access becomes practical. This is linked allocation made usable, and it is why the method survived in MS-DOS and in flash media.

**Indexed allocation.** Each file gets an **index block** holding the block addresses in order. *Advantages:* direct access needs only the index block plus the data block — **two accesses** — and there is no external fragmentation. *Disadvantages:* the index block is overhead even for a one-block file, and a single index block limits the file size, so schemes chain index blocks, use a multi-level index, or combine both.

**The Unix inode** is the combined scheme: a fixed number of **direct** pointers, then one **single indirect**, one **double indirect** and one **triple indirect** pointer. Small files — the overwhelming majority — are reached with the direct pointers and cost nothing extra; large files are still addressable, at the cost of extra index reads.

blocks.title: Worked example — maximum file size with a Unix inode
blocks.text:
A file system uses 4 KB blocks and 4-byte block pointers. An inode has **12 direct** pointers, one **single indirect**, one **double indirect** and one **triple indirect** pointer. What is the largest file?

First, how many pointers fit in one block?

$$\frac{4096\ \text{bytes}}{4\ \text{bytes}} = 1024 = 2^{10}\ \text{pointers per block}$$

Now count the data blocks each region reaches:

| Region | Data blocks | Bytes |
|---|---|---|
| 12 direct | $12$ | $12 \times 4\ \text{KB} = 48$ KB |
| single indirect | $1024$ | $1024 \times 4\ \text{KB} = 4$ MB |
| double indirect | $1024^{2} = 2^{20}$ | $2^{20} \times 4\ \text{KB} = 4$ GB |
| triple indirect | $1024^{3} = 2^{30}$ | $2^{30} \times 4\ \text{KB} = 4$ TB |

$$\text{Maximum} = 48\ \text{KB} + 4\ \text{MB} + 4\ \text{GB} + 4\ \text{TB} \approx 4.004\ \text{TB}$$

The triple-indirect region dominates so completely that 'approximately 4 TB' is the right answer, but write the exact sum when the options are close.

**Access cost for the same inode** (assume the inode is already in memory):

- a byte in the first 48 KB: **1** disk access;
- a byte in the single-indirect region: **2** (index block, then data);
- double indirect: **3**; triple indirect: **4**.

So the worst case is four reads for one byte — which is exactly why the buffer cache exists.

blocks.title: Worked example — comparing allocation methods on one operation
blocks.text:
A disk file occupies 100 blocks. We want to **insert a new block in the middle**, as block 51, and we must also be able to read block 75 directly.

**Contiguous.** Reading block 75: one access, $\text{start}+74$. Inserting in the middle: every block from 51 to 100 must be shifted, so about 50 reads and 50 writes — or the whole file is copied elsewhere. Roughly **100+ I/Os**.

**Linked.** Reading block 75: follow the chain from the start, **75 reads**. Inserting block 51: read forward to block 50 (50 reads), then write the new block and rewrite block 50's pointer — about **52 I/Os**, and no data is moved.

**Indexed.** Reading block 75: read the index block, then the data block — **2 accesses**. Inserting: read the index block, allocate a block, shift the entries after position 50 *within the index block* and write it back — about **3 I/Os**.

Indexed allocation wins on both counts, contiguous wins only on pure sequential streaming, and linked is competitive only when access is strictly sequential and the file grows at the end. These three columns are what match-the-following questions on this topic are built from.

## Free-space management

| Method | Representation | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| **Bit vector / bitmap** | one bit per block, 1 = free | simple, and finding the first free block is a fast word scan; the map must fit in memory, so it costs $\text{blocks}/8$ bytes |
| **Linked list** | each free block points to the next | no wasted space, but traversing to find $n$ contiguous blocks is expensive |
| **Grouping** | the first free block stores the addresses of $n$ free blocks, the last of which points to the next group | finds many free blocks quickly |
| **Counting** | store (first free block, run length) pairs | compact when free space is clustered, which it usually is |

For a 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks there are $2^{28}$ blocks, so the bitmap is $2^{28}/8 = 32$ MB — acceptable, and the reason bitmaps are the default.

## How I/O actually happens

Three techniques, in increasing order of CPU efficiency:

1. **Programmed I/O with polling.** The CPU repeatedly reads a status register until the device is ready, then transfers a byte or word itself. Simple, and a complete waste of the CPU.
2. **Interrupt-driven I/O.** The device raises an interrupt when ready; the CPU runs an interrupt service routine that moves the data. The CPU is free between transfers, but it still handles **every word**, so an interrupt per byte is unacceptable for a disk.
3. **Direct memory access (DMA).** The CPU programs a DMA controller with a source, a destination and a count, then goes away. The controller transfers the whole block directly between the device and memory and raises **one interrupt at the end**. The controller takes the bus for a cycle at a time, which is **cycle stealing**, so the CPU is slowed slightly but not interrupted.

Device registers are reached either by special I/O instructions on a separate address space (**port-mapped** or isolated I/O) or by ordinary loads and stores to reserved addresses (**memory-mapped** I/O — no special instructions, and the full addressing modes work).

**Buffering** (a holding area in memory) copes with speed mismatch between producer and consumer and with differing transfer sizes; double buffering lets one buffer fill while the other drains. **Caching** keeps a copy of data for reuse — the difference from a buffer is that a cache holds a *copy* of data that also exists elsewhere, while a buffer may hold the *only* copy. **Spooling** gives each job its own file for a device such as a printer that cannot interleave streams, and prints them one at a time.

blocks.q: A file system uses 1 KB blocks and 4-byte disk pointers. Using an inode with 10 direct, one single-indirect and one double-indirect pointer, the maximum file size is approximately
blocks.exp: One 1 KB block holds $1024/4 = 256$ pointers. Direct: $10 \times 1$ KB $= 10$ KB. Single indirect: $256 \times 1$ KB $= 256$ KB. Double indirect: $256^{2} \times 1$ KB $= 65536$ KB $= 64$ MB. The double-indirect region dominates, so the total is about 64 MB.

blocks.q: Which allocation method allows direct access to block $i$ in a constant number of disk accesses and causes no external fragmentation?
opts: Linked with a FAT stored on disk
blocks.exp: Indexed allocation reaches any block in two accesses — the index block and then the data block — and since blocks need not be adjacent there is no external fragmentation. Contiguous gives constant-time access but fragments; linked avoids fragmentation but costs $i+1$ accesses; an on-disk FAT still needs table reads unless it is cached.

tricks.title: Pointers per block first, then multiply
tricks.body: Every inode question starts with $P = \text{block size} / \text{pointer size}$. Then the regions contribute $d$, $P$, $P^{2}$ and $P^{3}$ blocks. Keep everything in powers of two and the arithmetic stays exact.

tricks.title: The largest region is almost the whole answer
tricks.body: The highest level of indirection contributes more than everything below it combined, so you can estimate the maximum file size from that term alone and only expand the full sum if two options are close.

tricks.title: Count accesses by counting levels
tricks.body: With the inode cached, reaching data costs 1 access in the direct region and $1 + (\text{levels of indirection})$ elsewhere. If the question says the inode is *not* in memory, add one more for the inode itself.

tricks.title: Match-the-following on allocation is three facts
tricks.body: Contiguous: fast direct access, external fragmentation, hard to grow. Linked: no direct access, no fragmentation, grows freely. Indexed: direct access, index overhead, no fragmentation. Every combination question is assembled from these nine statements.

traps.title: Buffering is not caching is not spooling
traps.body: A buffer smooths a speed or size mismatch and may hold the only copy. A cache holds a redundant copy for speed. A spool serialises access to a device that cannot be shared. Questions list all three as options for the same scenario.

traps.title: DMA does not eliminate interrupts
traps.body: It eliminates one interrupt *per word* and replaces them with one interrupt *per block*. An option saying DMA works without any CPU involvement at all is wrong — the CPU sets the transfer up and handles the completion interrupt.

traps.title: Hard links and reference counts
traps.body: Deleting a file with two hard links does not free the data; it decrements the inode's link count. Only when the count reaches zero is the space released. A symbolic link does not affect the count at all, which is why symbolic links can dangle.

topics.title: Protection and Security
topics.summary: Domains and access matrices, ACLs versus capabilities, program and system threats, and the cryptographic basics.

blocks.text:
## Protection and security are different problems

**Protection** is an internal mechanism: controlling what an already-authorised process may do to the objects of the system. **Security** is the broader question of whether the system's resources are used as intended, including defending against outsiders, physical theft and human error. A system can have perfect protection mechanisms and still be insecure because a user chose a weak password.

The goals are conventionally **confidentiality** (no unauthorised disclosure), **integrity** (no unauthorised modification) and **availability** (no denial of service). Two design principles matter more than the rest:

- **Principle of least privilege** — each user, process and program gets exactly the rights it needs for its job, for as long as it needs them, and no more. It limits the damage done by any bug or compromise.
- **Separation of mechanism and policy** — build a mechanism flexible enough to express many policies, then set the policy separately, because policies change and mechanisms are expensive to replace.

## Domains and the access matrix

A **protection domain** is a set of $\langle \text{object}, \text{rights} \rangle$ pairs. A process executes in a domain, and the domain can be a user, a process or a procedure. In Unix the domain is the (uid, gid) pair, and the **setuid** bit temporarily switches the domain during execution of a program — which is why setuid programs are the classic security hole.

The **access matrix** has one row per domain and one column per object, with the entry listing the allowed operations. It is the reference model for everything else:

| | file F1 | file F2 | printer | $D_2$ | $D_3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $D_1$ | read | — | — | switch | — |
| $D_2$ | — | read, write | print | — | switch |
| $D_3$ | read, execute | — | — | — | — |

Special rights make the matrix self-describing: **owner** (may add or remove rights in that object's column), **copy** (may pass a right to another domain, marked with an asterisk), **control** (may remove rights from another domain's row) and **switch** (may move to another domain).

The matrix is enormous and mostly empty, so it is never stored as a matrix. It is stored by slices:

- **By column — access control list (ACL).** Each object carries the list of domains and their rights. Answering *who may touch this file?* is instant; answering *what may this user touch?* requires scanning every object. Unix `rwx` bits are a compressed ACL with just three entries (owner, group, other).
- **By row — capability list.** Each domain carries a list of the objects it may touch, with the rights. A **capability** is an unforgeable ticket: possessing it *is* the authorisation. Answering *what may this process touch?* is instant; revoking a right from everybody is hard, because you must find every copy of the capability.
- **Lock-key** is a compromise: each object has locks, each domain has keys, and access is permitted when a key matches a lock.

**Revocation** is the discriminator. ACLs revoke easily (edit the object's list); capabilities need indirection, back-pointers, expiry or key invalidation. Any question contrasting the two is usually asking about revocation or about which direction of lookup is cheap.

## Threats

**Program threats** — the attacker gets legitimate code to misbehave.

| Threat | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Trojan horse | a program that does its advertised job *and* something hostile |
| Trap door (back door) | a deliberate hidden entry left by the author |
| Logic bomb | hostile code that triggers on a condition such as a date |
| **Stack/buffer overflow** | write past the end of a buffer to overwrite the saved return address and redirect execution into injected code |
| Virus | a fragment that embeds itself in a host program and spreads when that program runs; needs a host |

**System and network threats** — attacks on the system as a whole.

| Threat | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Worm** | a *standalone* program that copies itself across a network without a host program |
| Port scanning | probe for services with known vulnerabilities |
| Denial of service | consume a resource so legitimate users cannot |
| Distributed DoS | the same from many compromised hosts |
| Man in the middle | relay and possibly alter a conversation the parties believe is private |

The virus-versus-worm distinction is asked almost every time: a **virus needs a host program**, a **worm is self-contained and self-propagating**.

## Cryptography as a security tool

**Symmetric (secret-key)** encryption uses one key for both directions: DES (56-bit key, now broken by brute force), 3DES, AES (128/192/256-bit). It is fast, and suitable for bulk data — but $n$ mutually suspicious parties need $\binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)/2$ keys.

**Asymmetric (public-key)** encryption uses a key pair. Anyone may encrypt with the public key; only the private key decrypts. It is orders of magnitude slower, so real systems use it only to exchange a symmetric session key. $n$ parties need only $2n$ keys.

The two directions do different jobs:

- Encrypt with the **recipient's public** key $\Rightarrow$ **confidentiality** (only the recipient can read it).
- Encrypt (sign) with the **sender's private** key $\Rightarrow$ **authentication and non-repudiation** (only the sender could have produced it).

A **cryptographic hash** (SHA-256) maps any input to a fixed-size digest and must be one-way and collision-resistant; it gives **integrity**. A **digital signature** is a hash encrypted with the signer's private key — hashing first is what makes signing fast.

**Authentication** of users rests on something you know (password), something you have (token, smart card), or something you are (biometric). Passwords are stored **hashed and salted**; the salt is a per-user random value that makes precomputed rainbow tables useless and ensures two users with the same password get different stored hashes.

**Access-control models**: **DAC** (discretionary — the owner decides, as in Unix), **MAC** (mandatory — a system-wide policy with security labels that users cannot override), and **RBAC** (role-based — rights attach to roles and users are assigned roles, which is how least privilege is administered at scale).

blocks.title: Worked example — RSA with small numbers
blocks.text:
RSA is the standard public-key numerical. The steps:

1. Choose primes $p = 3$, $q = 11$. Then $n = pq = 33$.
2. $\phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1) = 2 \times 10 = 20$.
3. Choose $e$ with $1 < e < \phi(n)$ and $\gcd(e, \phi(n)) = 1$: take $e = 3$, since $\gcd(3,20)=1$.
4. Find $d$ with $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(n)}$: $3d \equiv 1 \pmod{20}$ gives $d = 7$, because $3 \times 7 = 21 = 20 + 1$.

Public key $(e, n) = (3, 33)$; private key $(d, n) = (7, 33)$.

**Encrypt $M = 5$:**

$$C = M^{e} \bmod n = 5^{3} \bmod 33 = 125 \bmod 33 = 125 - 99 = \mathbf{26}$$

**Decrypt $C = 26$:**

$$M = C^{d} \bmod n = 26^{7} \bmod 33$$

Do it by repeated squaring, using $26 \equiv -7 \pmod{33}$:

- $7^{2} = 49 \equiv 16$
- $7^{4} \equiv 16^{2} = 256 \equiv 256 - 231 = 25$
- $7^{6} \equiv 7^{4}\cdot 7^{2} \equiv 25 \times 16 = 400 \equiv 400 - 396 = 4$
- $7^{7} \equiv 4 \times 7 = 28$

Since the exponent 7 is odd, $26^{7} \equiv (-7)^{7} \equiv -28 \equiv 33 - 28 = \mathbf{5} \pmod{33}$.

The original message is recovered. Note that $e$ and $d$ are interchangeable in the arithmetic — that symmetry is exactly why the same algorithm serves for both encryption and signing.

blocks.q: To provide confidentiality, a sender encrypts a message with
blocks.exp: Only the receiver holds the matching private key, so only the receiver can decrypt — that is confidentiality. Encrypting with the *sender's private* key gives the opposite property, authentication, because anyone can verify it with the sender's public key but nobody else could have created it.

blocks.q: An access matrix stored by columns gives
blocks.exp: A column of the matrix is one object together with every domain's rights over it, which is precisely an access control list attached to that object. A *row* — one domain and everything it may touch — is a capability list. ACLs make revocation easy; capabilities make per-process lookup fast.

tricks.title: Row equals capability, column equals ACL
tricks.body: Remember it by what each answers quickly: a row answers 'what can this subject do?' (a capability list the process carries), a column answers 'who can touch this object?' (an ACL the object carries). Revocation is easy exactly in the ACL case.

tricks.title: Private key encrypts for signing, public key encrypts for secrecy
tricks.body: Ask what the attacker must not be able to do. If the answer is 'read it', use the receiver's public key. If the answer is 'forge it', use the sender's private key. Doing both means encrypting twice.

tricks.title: Virus needs a host, worm does not
tricks.body: One word decides most malware questions. A second discriminator: a worm spreads by itself over a network, a virus waits for a user to run the infected program.

traps.title: Authentication is not authorisation
traps.body: Authentication establishes who you are; authorisation decides what you may do. The access matrix is an authorisation mechanism; passwords and biometrics are authentication mechanisms.

traps.title: Salting does not make hashing stronger
traps.body: A salt does not make a single password harder to crack. It defeats *precomputation* — one rainbow table can no longer attack all accounts at once — and hides the fact that two users chose the same password.

traps.title: Public-key cryptography is not used for bulk data
traps.body: Because it is far slower than symmetric encryption, real protocols use public-key methods only to agree a session key and then switch to AES. An option claiming that public-key encryption replaces symmetric encryption is wrong.

topics.title: Virtual Machines, Linux, Windows and Distributed Systems
topics.summary: Hypervisors and containers, what makes Linux and Windows different, and the core ideas of distributed operating systems.

blocks.text:
## Virtual machines

A **virtual machine monitor (hypervisor)** gives each guest the illusion of its own complete machine: its own CPU, memory and devices. The guest OS runs believing it is in kernel mode, while in reality the hypervisor holds that privilege and traps the guest's privileged instructions — the **trap-and-emulate** technique.

| Type | Runs on | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Type 1 (bare metal, native)** | directly on the hardware | Xen, VMware ESXi, Hyper-V |
| **Type 2 (hosted)** | as a process on a host OS | VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, QEMU |

**Full virtualisation** runs an unmodified guest. **Paravirtualisation** modifies the guest to call the hypervisor explicitly (hypercalls), which is faster but requires guest cooperation — the original Xen design. **Hardware-assisted virtualisation** (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) adds a mode below kernel mode so that privileged guest instructions trap cleanly, removing the awkward cases in the x86 instruction set where a privileged instruction silently failed instead of trapping.

The **Popek and Goldberg** criterion states that an architecture is virtualisable if every *sensitive* instruction (one that changes or depends on the machine's configuration) is also *privileged*. The classic x86 was not virtualisable by this test, which is why binary translation and then hardware assistance were needed.

**Containers** are not virtual machines. They share the host kernel and isolate processes using namespaces (separate views of the process table, file system, network) and control groups (resource limits). The consequences: containers start in milliseconds and have almost no overhead, but they cannot run a different kernel and offer weaker isolation than a hypervisor.

Memory management under virtualisation needs a second translation — guest virtual to guest physical to host physical — done either by **shadow page tables** in software or by **nested paging** (EPT/NPT) in hardware.

Benefits of virtualisation: consolidation of many servers onto one machine, complete isolation between guests, snapshots and live migration, and the ability to run several operating systems and to develop for one platform on another.

## Linux and Windows

**Linux** is a **monolithic kernel with loadable modules**: the whole kernel shares one address space for speed, but drivers and file systems can be inserted and removed at run time without rebuilding. Key facts worth knowing:

- Processes and threads are both created by `clone()`, which takes flags saying what to share; a thread is simply a task that shares the address space and file table. The kernel schedules **tasks**, so the process/thread distinction is largely a user-space convention.
- The default scheduler is the **Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS)**, which tracks each task's **virtual runtime** and always runs the task with the smallest, using a red-black tree rather than fixed queues. There is no fixed time quantum; the slice depends on the number of runnable tasks and the task's weight (derived from its nice value). Real-time tasks use separate SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR classes at higher priority.
- File systems: ext2 (no journal), ext3 and ext4 (journalled), with the **virtual file system (VFS)** layer giving a common interface so that any file system can be mounted anywhere in the single tree.
- Everything is a file: devices appear in `/dev`, kernel state in `/proc` and `/sys`.

**Windows NT and its descendants** use a **hybrid** design: a small kernel and a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) at the bottom, with the executive above it providing the object manager, virtual memory, process and I/O managers, and with environment subsystems in user mode. Its scheduler is preemptive with 32 priority levels (16–31 real time, 1–15 variable, 0 for the zero page thread), boosting priority after I/O completion and lowering it when a thread exhausts its quantum. **NTFS** is journalled and stores everything, including its own metadata, in the Master File Table.

## Distributed systems

A **distributed system** is a collection of independent machines that appears to its users as one system. The interesting problems all come from two facts: there is **no shared memory** and there is **no global clock**.

**Transparency** is the design goal, and it has several kinds — access (local and remote objects are used the same way), location (the name does not reveal where the object is), migration, replication, concurrency and failure transparency.

**Logical clocks.** Because physical clocks drift, Lamport defined the **happens-before** relation $a \to b$ and a counter rule: increment the local counter before each event, attach it to every message, and on receipt set $C = \max(C, C_{\text{msg}}) + 1$. This guarantees $a \to b \Rightarrow C(a) < C(b)$, but **not** the converse — two unrelated (concurrent) events can have ordered timestamps. **Vector clocks** fix exactly that: $V(a) < V(b)$ if and only if $a \to b$.

**Distributed mutual exclusion.**

| Algorithm | Messages per entry | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Centralised coordinator | 3 (request, grant, release) | single point of failure, bottleneck |
| Ricart–Agrawala (distributed) | $2(n-1)$ | every node must be up; $n$ points of failure |
| Token ring | 1 to $\infty$ | lost token must be regenerated |

**Election algorithms** choose a new coordinator after a failure. The **bully** algorithm has the highest-numbered live process win, at a cost of $O(n^{2})$ messages in the worst case. The **ring** algorithm circulates an election message collecting process ids and costs $O(n)$ messages but takes longer.

**Remote procedure call (RPC)** makes a network request look like a function call: a client **stub** marshals the arguments (handling byte-order differences via an external data representation), sends them, and unmarshals the reply. Because messages can be lost, RPC offers semantics of *at most once* or *exactly once*; true exactly-once requires the server to remember duplicate requests.

**Distributed file systems** such as NFS make remote files appear local through mounting; NFS is stateless in its classic version, which makes crash recovery simple but complicates locking.

blocks.title: Worked example — message cost of distributed mutual exclusion
blocks.text:
A distributed system has $n = 12$ nodes, and one critical-section entry is requested.

**Centralised.** The requester sends one REQUEST to the coordinator, receives one REPLY, and sends one RELEASE afterwards: $3$ messages, independent of $n$. The coordinator handles all traffic, so it is both a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

**Ricart–Agrawala.** The requester timestamps a REQUEST and sends it to all $n-1 = 11$ others, then waits for 11 REPLY messages: $2(n-1) = 22$ messages. The delay before entry is one round trip, and **every** node must be alive — if any one has crashed, its silence is indistinguishable from a denial, so the algorithm turns $1$ point of failure into $n$.

**Token ring.** If the token happens to arrive immediately, 1 message suffices; if the node has just passed it on, the token must travel all the way round, costing up to $n = 12$ hops; and if no node wants the critical section, the token circulates forever, consuming bandwidth with 0 useful entries.

So for $n = 12$: **3** versus **22** versus **1 to 12**. The centralised scheme is the cheapest in messages and the worst in fault tolerance — the standard trade-off of the whole field.

blocks.q: Which statement about containers and virtual machines is correct?
opts: Containers include a full guest operating system, virtual machines do not
Containers share the host kernel; virtual machines run their own kernel
Containers provide stronger isolation than virtual machines
blocks.exp: A container is a group of processes isolated by kernel namespaces and cgroups, so it uses the host's kernel and cannot run a different one. A virtual machine is given emulated hardware and boots its own kernel, which costs far more memory and start-up time but isolates more strongly.

blocks.q: In Lamport's logical clocks, if $C(a) < C(b)$ for two events $a$ and $b$, then
opts: no conclusion about ordering can be drawn
blocks.exp: Lamport clocks guarantee only the forward implication: $a \to b$ implies $C(a) < C(b)$. The converse fails, because two concurrent events on different machines can receive any ordered pair of timestamps. Deciding causality from timestamps alone requires vector clocks.

tricks.title: Type 1 sits on metal, type 2 sits on an OS
tricks.body: If the question mentions a host operating system, it is type 2 (hosted). If the hypervisor boots the machine itself, it is type 1. Performance questions always favour type 1.

tricks.title: Lamport gives one direction only
tricks.body: $a \to b \Rightarrow C(a) < C(b)$, never the reverse. Any option that reads a causal order off Lamport timestamps is wrong; only vector clocks are bidirectional.

tricks.title: Message counts are worth memorising
tricks.body: Centralised 3, Ricart–Agrawala $2(n-1)$, token ring 1 to $n$ (or unbounded when idle), bully $O(n^{2})$, ring election $O(n)$. These five numbers answer most distributed-algorithm questions directly.

traps.title: Paravirtualisation requires modifying the guest
traps.body: Full virtualisation runs an unmodified guest; paravirtualisation does not. An option offering paravirtualisation as the way to run an unmodified legacy OS is wrong.

traps.title: A distributed system is not a multiprocessor
traps.body: Multiprocessors share memory and a clock; distributed systems share neither and communicate only by messages. Almost every difficulty in the topic — ordering, agreement, failure detection — comes from that one distinction.

traps.title: CFS has no time quantum
traps.body: Linux's Completely Fair Scheduler picks the task with the least virtual runtime rather than cycling through a queue with a fixed slice. Describing it as round robin with priorities is inaccurate; the target latency is divided among runnable tasks in proportion to their weights.
